hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.story:
Hawaii is a chain of Pacific islands that is now a state of the United States. For most of the 19th century it was an independent country. Kamehameha I conquered the islands between 1795 and 1810 and formed the Kingdom of Hawaii, and the United States and other powers formally recognised it. Disease and war cut the Native Hawaiian population by about 90 percent in the first century after contact with the West, down to 53,900 in 1876. American missionaries arrived in 1820 and gained great influence.

The sovereignty movement rests on what happened next. On 17 January 1893 a group made up mostly of Americans living in the kingdom overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, with the support of armed sailors landed from the warship USS Boston. An inquiry for President Grover Cleveland found that the American minister had helped the plotters and that most of the population opposed them, and a second report in 1894 cleared everyone except the queen. The plotters' government became the Republic of Hawaii in 1894. In 1898 the United States annexed the islands, and Native Hawaiians had no say in it. The movement regards both the overthrow and the annexation as illegal.

The modern movement grew in the 1960s and 1970s alongside other Indigenous campaigns. Its grievances included commercial development, corruption in the Hawaiian Homelands program, building on burial grounds and the bombing of Kahoʻolawe island.

It is a set of groups with different aims. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, started in 1987, runs like a government in waiting, with a constitution, elected offices, representatives for each island and Mililani Trask as its first governor. It reported 21,000 members in 1997 and led 10,000 people on a march to Iolani Palace in 1993, the 100th anniversary of the overthrow. The Nation of Hawaiʻi, led by Dennis "Bumpy" Kanahele, wants a republic where other groups prefer restoring the monarchy. It occupied the area around Makapuʻu lighthouse in 1989 and Kaupo Beach in 1993. It ended the second occupation in exchange for land in Waimānalo, where it built a village, a cultural centre and a puʻuhonua, a place of refuge. In 1995 the group sheltered an activist who refused to pay federal taxes, and Kanahele served eight months in federal prison and was barred for a time from the village. The state may negotiate over land, and federal criminal law still applies on it.

In 1993 Congress passed the Apology Resolution, which acknowledged that the overthrow was illegal. An apology is a statement and returned no land and no power. The next step offered was the Akaka Bill, first proposed in 2000, which would have begun federal recognition of a Native Hawaiian government, much like the relationship Native American tribes have with Washington. Under that model a people governs some of its own affairs while staying inside the United States. Many sovereignty groups opposed it because it would have treated past land transfers as valid, and Trask objected to its 20-year limit on claims against the United States. A 2005 Grassroot Institute poll found most Hawaii residents opposed it too.

In 2015 the Interior Department announced a procedure for recognising a Native Hawaiian government. A nonprofit planned an election of convention delegates, and that November Justice Anthony Kennedy halted the counting of the votes. Hawaii remains a state, and the groups remain divided between recognition within the United States and full independence. The case shows that winning an admission of wrongdoing from a government and winning back the power to rule are separate things, and a people seeking the second needs new law or a new negotiation.

kingitanga.story:
The Kīngitanga, or Māori King Movement, is a line of Māori monarchs in New Zealand, based at Tūrangawaewae marae in Ngāruawāhia, in the Waikato region of the central North Island. It began in the 1850s as a rival authority to British colonial rule and still exists today.

The background is land. Under the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840, Māori chiefs and the British Crown agreed to a relationship whose meaning is still argued over. By the 1850s European settlers outnumbered Māori and wanted farmland. Government land buyers made offers to single chiefs or small groups of owners, which set Māori against one another. In May 1854 as many as 2,000 leaders met in south Taranaki and heard speakers urge a common refusal to sell. Tāmihana Te Rauparaha, who had met Queen Victoria in England in 1851, came home with the idea of one Māori king over all the tribes. A monarch equal in standing to the queen, the reasoning went, could deal with Europeans on equal terms.

Several chiefs declined the role. Wiremu Tamihana, the chief known as the kingmaker, proposed the elderly Waikato chief Te Wherowhero, who was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858 as Pōtatau Te Wherowhero. Day to day, the movement worked much like a government. It had a flag, a council of state, a code of laws, magistrates, police, a surveyor, a bank and a newspaper called Te Hokioi. Pōtatau proposed a boundary at Maungatautari, with himself ruling land still held under Māori custom and the governor ruling land the Crown had acquired. Support was strongest in Waikato. Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Porou and Tūhoe have never joined. In 1861 Tamihana wrote that Māori were a separate nation.

On 9 July 1863 Governor George Grey ordered all Māori living between Auckland and the Waikato to swear allegiance to Queen Victoria or leave for the south of the Waikato River. Troops crossed into Waikato three days later. After defeats including Ōrākau in 1864, the second king, Tāwhiao, and his followers withdrew into the land of the Ngāti Maniapoto tribe, later called the King Country. They declared that Europeans crossing its boundary, the aukati, risked death. Parliament passed laws to seize the land of those it called rebels, and 486,500 hectares were taken, including farmed land and burial sites.

The King Country stayed closed to government for about 20 years. Tāwhiao renounced war in the late 1860s and refused to join a renewed fight. The government wanted a railway through the centre of the island, and Tāwhiao turned down its offer of land and aid in 1878. In July 1881 he and 70 followers laid down their guns at Alexandra, now Pirongia, and declared peace.

The movement continues, centred on the Waikato-Tainui tribes. The monarch has no legal or judicial power under New Zealand law. Nga wai hono i te po, daughter of King Tuheitia, became the eighth monarch in September 2024. The legal argument has also continued. In 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal, which hears Māori claims against the Crown, concluded that the chiefs who signed the Māori text of the treaty in February 1840 did not give up their authority to make and enforce law, and agreed to share power with the governor. The tribunal said nothing about how and when the Crown gained the sovereignty it now holds, except that it did not come from an informed handover by those chiefs.

The case shows a people who built the working parts of a state and lost much of their land to invasion once the colonial government treated that as a challenge. The monarchy still exists, without the power to rule territory.

mcgirt-v-oklahoma.story:
McGirt v. Oklahoma is a 2020 ruling by the United States Supreme Court about who may prosecute crimes across much of eastern Oklahoma. To follow it, a reader needs to know how American law treats tribal land. An Indian reservation is land Congress has set aside for a Native nation, and the law calls such land Indian country. Inside it, tribal and federal authorities handle many matters that a state would handle elsewhere. A federal law called the Major Crimes Act says that when a Native American commits one of the serious crimes it lists in Indian country, the federal courts try the case and the state courts do not.

Before Oklahoma became a state in 1907, about half its land, including today's Tulsa area, belonged to the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations, which had been forced there from the eastern United States along the Trail of Tears. Congress broke up much of their land into individual plots and passed a 1906 law that spoke of dissolving the tribal governments, while the same law kept them in force. For more than a century Oklahoma acted as though the reservations had ended.

The test case came from a prisoner. Jimcy McGirt, a member of the Seminole Nation, was convicted by an Oklahoma court in 1997 of sex crimes against a child in Broken Arrow and sentenced to life without parole plus 1,000 years. He argued that the crime took place on the Muscogee reservation, so the state had never had the power to try him. A similar case, brought by a Muscogee man named Patrick Murphy, had already reached the court, and Justice Neil Gorsuch had stepped aside from it because he had dealt with it as a lower court judge.

Gorsuch wrote the 5 to 4 decision. The rule he applied is simple. A reservation set up by Congress lasts until Congress clearly ends it. Allotting the land and pushing the tribe aside over the years do not count. The treaties promised the land, Congress had never said otherwise, and so the government was held to its word. Chief Justice John Roberts dissented. Oklahoma's Court of Criminal Appeals then applied the same reasoning to nine other Indigenous nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country.

The results reached the courthouse quickly. About 1,900 prisoners in Oklahoma fit the conditions of the ruling, though only around 10 percent qualified for a new hearing. Courts began throwing out old convictions and passing the cases to federal prosecutors. Less than a year later the state appeals court ruled that McGirt did not apply to old cases, which stopped that. An FBI agent working in Oklahoma said many cases handed over were going unprosecuted, and the state argued that tribal and federal offices lacked the staff. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that state courts share power with federal courts over crimes by non-Indians against Indian victims in Indian country, which took back part of what the state had lost.

For someone thinking about founding a territory, McGirt shows both the strength and the limit of old paper. A 19th-century promise can still bind a modern government if it was made by the right body and never properly withdrawn, and that took more than a century to establish. What it decided was which American court hears which case. The nations did not become independent states, and federal law still governs the land. A claimant with no treaty from Congress has nothing comparable to rely on.

nunavut.story:
Nunavut is Canada's largest territory, covering 2,093,190 square kilometres of the Arctic. Canada has provinces, which hold their own powers under the constitution, and territories, which get their powers from laws passed by the national parliament. Until 1999 this land was part of the Northwest Territories. It became its own territory because the Inuit, the Indigenous people of the region, negotiated for it.

In the 1970s Inuit organisations were pressing for recognition of their rights and for a settlement of their land claim, meaning their claim to land they had never formally given up. In 1976, during those talks, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and the federal government discussed splitting the Northwest Territories to give the Inuit a territory where they would be the majority. On 14 April 1982 a vote across the Northwest Territories backed division, and the federal government gave conditional agreement seven months later.

The land-claims agreement was finished in September 1992, and nearly 85 percent of voters in the area ratified it. On 9 July 1993 Parliament passed two laws, the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act. One settled the claim and the other set up the government. There was then a transition of nearly six years, and the territory began on 1 April 1999, with Iqaluit as its capital. The whole process took about 23 years from the first proposal.

In 2021 Nunavut had 36,858 people, of whom 84 percent were Inuit, and an estimated 43,091 in late 2026. Official languages are Inuktut, the Inuit language, along with English and French. Its assembly is elected without political parties and chooses a premier from among its members, and a council of elders advises on using Inuit knowledge in government. For its first 25 years the federal government kept control of public land and resources. A devolution agreement signed on 18 January 2024 hands that control to the territorial government.

Nunavut makes no claim to be a state. Its people remain Canadian citizens under Canadian law, and the territory exists because Parliament said so. The case shows what negotiation can achieve when a people has a recognised claim and a government willing to talk. It produced a government run by the local majority over an area larger than most countries, in exchange for staying inside the country, and it needed the consent of voters and of Parliament at every step.

sami-parliaments.story:
The Sámi are an Indigenous people whose homeland, Sápmi, stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. They were there before those borders. From the Middle Ages the northern kingdoms and Russia expanded into Sámi land, and in some areas Sámi paid tax to two states at once. Most Sámi settled in villages from the 16th century onward, while others kept to semi-nomadic reindeer herding. Today they elect their own parliaments in three of the four countries.

Norway's came out of a fight over a dam. In 1978 a state plan for a hydroelectric dam on the Alta river would have flooded the Sámi village of Máze. Strong opposition led to meetings with the government in 1980 and 1981, and a committee on Sámi rights proposed an elected Sámi body. The Sámi Act followed in 1987, and the Norwegian parliament opened on 9 October 1989 in Karasjok, with 39 members from seven voting districts covering the whole country. Sweden's opened on 26 August 1993 in Kiruna, with 31 members. Its actions must follow decisions of the Riksdag, Sweden's national parliament. Finland held a trial election in 1972 and set up an elected Sámi delegation the next year, and that body was replaced on 2 March 1996 by a parliament of 21 members in Inari.

All three hold elections every four years, separate from national elections. A person votes on the basis of identity and language. In Sweden, for example, a voter must identify as Sámi and speak a Sámi language or have a parent or grandparent who did. In 2021, 9,220 people were registered to vote there. The parliaments work on language, culture and Sámi status as an Indigenous people, and Finland's divides the public money set aside for Sámi use and can propose bills. They have no separate territory, no police and no power over non-Sámi neighbours. This is called cultural autonomy, meaning self-rule over a people's own affairs without control of an area of land.

In Russia a Kola Sámi Assembly was set up on 12 December 2010 in Murmansk, but as of 2017 the authorities did not recognise it as a lawmaking body. The parliaments cooperate through a Sámi Parliamentary Council, and a Conference of Sámi Parliamentarians has met every three years since 2005. None claims independence. The case shows a form of self-government that can cross borders because it attaches to people and leaves the land under existing states, and how much it can do depends on what each host country's law allows.

ada-kaleh.story:
Ada Kaleh was an inhabited island in the River Danube, about 1.75 kilometres long and half a kilometre wide, roughly 3 kilometres downstream of Orșova on what is now the border of Romania and Serbia. Its name comes from Turkish words meaning island fortress. The Danube there was a frontier between two empires, Austria and the Ottoman Empire, the Turkish-ruled state based in Constantinople, and they fought over the island's fortress for a century. It passed to the Ottomans in 1699, back to the Austrians in the war of 1716 to 1718, to the Ottomans after a four-month siege in 1738, and to the Austrians again in 1789. A 1791 treaty returned it to the Ottomans.

The people who lived there were mostly Turkish-speaking Muslims. An Ottoman document says they descended from the families of soldiers stationed in the fort. Others arrived later, including 179 Muslim Roma refugees after the war of 1877 to 1878, who at first had no homes and lived in the arches beneath the fortress.

That war produced the odd legal position. The Ottomans lost the land on both banks, and when peace was negotiated at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, the delegates forgot the island. A territory passes to a new ruler only if someone gives it up or takes it, and nobody had done either. So it stayed Ottoman in law for 45 years, with Austria-Hungary on one side of the river and Serbia on the other.

Daily life followed from that. The Ottoman government kept sending an administrator and a judge. Residents were Ottoman citizens, paid no tax or customs, were not drafted into any army, and voted in the Ottoman elections of 1908. The island became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest. People made Turkish delight, baklava, rose water and rose oil, and worked in tobacco, fishing and later tourism. Men wore the fez, and the island was known for Turkish oil wrestling.

Austria-Hungary's army occupied the island in 1913 and declared sovereignty, and Romania occupied it in 1919. The Ottoman Empire did not accept these moves. The Treaty of Lausanne settled the matter in 1923 and made the island Romanian. Many families then left for Turkey over the years that followed, and in 1951 some were forced to resettle on the Bărăgan Plain.

Under Communist rule Romania and Yugoslavia built the Iron Gates hydroelectric dam on the Danube. The remaining Turkish residents had left by 1967, mostly for Turkey and some for Dobruja in Romania. In 1970 the reservoir flooded the island, and it now lies under water.

The case shows a real gap in the map, which is rare and comes from a mistake by those drawing it. It lasted only because a recognised state already held the title and kept sending officials. The people there gained freedom from their neighbours' taxes and armies because of that old title, and a later treaty ended the arrangement.

caspian-convention-2018.story:
The Caspian is a huge body of salt water between Europe and Asia, with a surface of about 371,000 square kilometres, an area similar to Japan. It has no outlet to the ocean. Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan surround it. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea is the treaty those five signed in 2018 to say who controls what on it.

For decades they argued over a question that sounds like geography and is really about money and power, namely whether the Caspian counts as a sea or a lake. The United Nations law of the sea applies to seas. It would give each coastal country a band of territorial water and a wider zone of resources, leaving the middle open to the ships of the whole world. Lakes have no such general rules, so neighbours divide them by agreement, as with a shared border lake. Which label applied would change who got which oil and gas under the water.

For most of the 20th century the question hardly arose. Under a treaty between Iran and the Soviet Union the Caspian was treated as a lake split into two sectors, Iranian and Soviet, with fish shared. When the Soviet Union ended, Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan replaced it on the northern shores, and oil and gas became the main prize. Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan made deals with each other using median lines, meaning lines halfway between shores. Iran wanted one deal among all five and aimed for a one-fifth share. Iranian patrol boats at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed oil fields, and Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan quarrelled as well.

After talks running from about 1990, the five leaders signed the convention at Aktau, Kazakhstan, on 12 August 2018. It treats the Caspian as neither one thing nor the other. Each country gets 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water, which it fully controls, and 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) more of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface is common space open to the five. The seabed, which holds the oil and gas, is left to deals between neighbouring countries.

The convention takes effect only when all five ratify it, meaning approve it formally at home. Four have. Iran's cabinet approved it on 22 July 2026 and sent it to parliament, which had not ratified it as of September 2026. Until then the treaty is signed but not binding.

For anyone thinking of building or anchoring out there, the open middle of the Caspian differs from the open ocean. On the high seas every country's ships have freedoms under international law, and those freedoms are what people planning sea colonies rely on. Here the middle belongs in common to five named countries, an outsider has no such freedom, and the deal shows that coastal states can write their own rules for an enclosed body of water.
caspian-convention-2018.why: Surface area changed from 389,000 to about 371,000 square km, the figure in the Caspian Sea article excluding the Garabogazköl lagoon; 389,000 does not appear in the listed source.

kasikili-sedudu-icj.story:
Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 square kilometres in the Chobe River on the border between Botswana and Namibia in southern Africa. No one lives there permanently, and floods cover it for several months a year from about March. It is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area.

The dispute came from a colonial document. In 1890 Germany and Britain signed the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty to settle their colonies in what are now Namibia and Botswana. The treaty said the line should follow the thalweg of the "main channel" of the Chobe. A thalweg is the deepest line of a river, the path boats follow. The river splits in two around the island, and the treaty did not say which branch was the main one. If it was the north branch the island lay in Botswana's half, and if it was the south branch the island lay in Namibia's.

When colonies became countries they inherited such lines, and the wording became their problem. On 17 May 1996 the two countries sent a joint letter to the International Court of Justice, the United Nations court for disputes between countries. Such a court can decide only if both sides agree to come, and they had signed a special agreement to do that. They asked it to decide the boundary under the 1890 treaty and the island's status.

Since the treaty gave no definition, the court worked one out from the river itself. It compared the two channels on depth, width, the volume of water they carried, the shape of the riverbed and whether boats could use them, looking at surveys from different periods. In 1999 it held that the northern channel was the main one. The border therefore follows the deepest line north of the island, which places Sedudu in Botswana.

The case shows how such quarrels really end. A river island is not empty land waiting for a claimant, because some treaty line already covers it. Even a vague colonial phrase binds the countries that inherited it, and the only open question is which of them holds the place. The two countries agreed in advance to put the question to a court, and only countries can bring a case there.

lake-constance-no-border.story:
Lake Constance is a large lake on the River Rhine at the northern foot of the Alps, where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet. Its main upper part covers about 473 square kilometres and its lower part about 63. Towns line the shore, among them Constance, Friedrichshafen, Bregenz and Lindau, and the lake supplies drinking water to southwestern Germany. Its shores belong to the German states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria, the Swiss cantons of St. Gallen, Thurgau and Schaffhausen, and the Austrian state of Vorarlberg. No treaty says where the borders run across most of the water.

Areas less than 25 metres deep are treated as belonging to the nearest country. Beyond that depth, no legally binding agreement exists, and each country holds its own view. Switzerland holds that the line goes down the middle of the lake. Austria says the deep part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement known as a condominium, meaning shared rule. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous.

Daily life carries on because the practical questions have been separated from the border question. Shipping and fishing are handled by separate treaties. A shared shipping ordinance sets the rules for all boats, the German, Swiss and Austrian water police patrol, and all boats must be registered. Commercial fishing lands about 1.5 million kilograms of fish a year. Nobody has needed to settle the line in order to run any of this.

A person might read "no agreed border" as meaning the middle of the lake belongs to no one. That reading fails. Under each of the three views the deep water belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so the only question is which of them, and an outsider who anchored a platform there would be subject to the same police and shipping rules as any other boat. The question remains unsettled, and the lake shows how neighbours can leave a line undrawn for as long as they cooperate.

migingo-island.story:
Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 square metres in Lake Victoria in East Africa, smaller than a soccer pitch and one of the most crowded islands on earth. Lake Victoria is shared by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. What makes Migingo valuable is the Nile perch, a large food fish, in the waters around it. The boundary was set in colonial times, when Britain ruled both Kenya and Uganda. A 1926 order, the Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council, draws a straight line across the water between named islands, and that wording was later copied into Uganda's constitution. Maps have shown Migingo on the Kenyan side since then.

Nobody paid it much attention for decades. Two Kenyan fishermen, Dalmas Tembo and George Kibebe, say they settled it in 1991, when it was covered in weeds and home to birds and snakes. A Ugandan fisherman, Joseph Nsubuga, says he arrived in 2004 and found only an abandoned house. Fishermen from Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania followed. Kenya says Ugandan marine police pitched a tent and raised a flag there in June 2004. Police from both countries occupied it at various times after that.

In February 2009 Kenyans living on the rock were told to buy special Ugandan permits, which set off a diplomatic row. By then it held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino, and about 500 people. On 13 March 2009 ministers met in Kampala and agreed that fishermen could carry on working until experts fixed the boundary, and that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers. A visit two weeks later ended in insults because the police had stayed. A Kenyan minister called the Ugandan delegation hyenas, and the Ugandans said they would take down the flag only after consulting their president.

Uganda proposed a survey using the 1926 order. In May, President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda conceded the island was Kenyan while saying Kenyan fishermen were fishing illegally in Ugandan waters, which come within about 510 metres of the rock. Much of the quarrel is over fishing rights, so the water matters as much as the rock. A joint survey began on 2 June. Sources differ on what came next. Wikipedia says the results in late July placed Migingo 510 metres inside Kenya and that Uganda lowered its flag and withdrew. A Kenya News Agency report in January 2025 says the joint work stopped in early July when surveyors disagreed, that the Kenyan team later reached the 510-metre figure, and that the report was still unpublished.

The dispute still affects the residents. On 2 January 2025 people working and living on Migingo petitioned President William Ruto to publish the 2009 report, saying Ugandan security forces had been harassing and arresting Kenyans since 2004. In August 2025 Kenyan fishermen said Ugandan security officials were still seizing their gear.

The case separates two ideas that people often run together. Settling first, raising a flag and even running a town on a rock did not change who owned it, because the old line decided that. And a line on paper did not stop a neighbour's armed officers from controlling the place. Someone living there depends on which government has boats on the water that day, whatever the survey says.

pheasant-island.story:
Pheasant Island is a small uninhabited island in the Bidasoa river, the border between Spain and France at the western end of the Pyrenees, between the towns of Irun and Hendaye. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres, with an area of under one hectare, and it was eroding. Spain and France take turns governing it, changing every six months.

The arrangement comes from a peace negotiation. In 1659 it hosted 24 meetings between Spain's minister Luis Méndez de Haro and France's Cardinal Mazarin, and these ended in the Treaty of the Pyrenees. King Louis XIV of France married Maria Theresa of Spain as part of the peace, and in 1660 she said farewell to her father, Philip IV of Spain, on the island before crossing into France.

Under the treaty the island is a condominium, meaning two countries share sovereignty over it, and it is the smallest in the world. The naval commander at Hondarribia in Spain governs it from 1 February to 31 July. A French official governs it from 1 August to 31 January. That official's ordinary job concerns the sea and coast of the region, and the post carries the title "viceroy of Pheasant Island".

In practice the mayors of Irun and Hendaye look after it. Municipal staff land every six months to clean and garden, and naval personnel from San Sebastián and Bayonne check it every five days. Nobody lives there, and access is forbidden apart from rare heritage open days, though at low tide it can sometimes be reached on foot from the Spanish side.

The case matters to anyone hoping to find a place between two countries. A strip of land sitting exactly on a border looks as if it might belong to no one. Here the opposite is true, because two states hold the title at once and officials of both have the right to remove a visitor. The arrangement has lasted for more than three centuries and still operates.

santa-rosa-island-amazon.story:
Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon River at the point where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, across the water from Leticia in Colombia and Tabatinga in Brazil. There are no bridges, because the river is wide and floods often and its banks keep moving, so almost everyone travels by boat. About 3,000 people live there. Peruvians from the surrounding province founded the settlement on 30 August 1974. It serves as Peru's border checkpoint for the area, and its economy rests on river trade, tourism and fishing.

Rivers make awkward borders because they move. Peru and Colombia drew their line in treaties from 1922 and 1929, and islands in the Amazon form and vanish over time. A treaty signed a century ago cannot name an island that did not exist yet, and that is the core of this dispute.

For decades Peru ran the place. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made the island a district of its Loreto region, with its own local government. On 5 August 2025 Colombian President Gustavo Petro wrote on social media that Peru had "appropriated it by law", and he warned that the change could cut Leticia, a town of nearly 60,000 people, off from the river. Petro's concern is that Leticia's use as an Amazon port depends on the channel beside it.

The two sides read the same treaties differently. Peru treats the island as an extension of Chinería Island, which the treaties did cover, so to Peru it is old Peruvian land. Colombia answers that Santa Rosa had not yet formed when the treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. It also argues that the border follows the deepest line of the Amazon and that new islands have formed on its side of that line. Colombia's foreign ministry says the two countries need to work together on deciding who holds each island.

The island remains under Peruvian administration and disputed by Colombia. The case shows that new land in a border river does not become free for the taking. When a river produces an island, the neighbouring countries attach it to their own law, and a person hoping to claim it would find two governments already asserting it.

abaco.story:
The Abaco Islands are an inhabited chain in the northern Bahamas, the group of Atlantic islands just east of Florida. In the early 1970s the Bahamas was preparing to leave British rule, and it became independent in 1973. Some white residents of Abaco objected to living under black rule. The Abaco Independence Movement was founded in mid-1973 (sources differ between June and August) by Chuck Hall and Bert Williams, with the stated aim of self-determination for Abaco through legal and peaceful political action, within a federal Bahamas.

Hall and Williams contacted Michael Oliver, a real-estate millionaire based in the United States. Oliver's Phoenix Foundation backed libertarian attempts to create new states, meaning states with very little government. In 1972 it had piled sand on a reef in the South Pacific and declared the Republic of Minerva, and Tonga sent an expedition and raised its own flag there within days. Abaco was the foundation's next attempt, and in 1980 it backed a breakaway on Espiritu Santo in Vanuatu.

The foundation paid for a newsletter, The Abaco Independent. The movement proposed placing all Crown land on Abaco, meaning land held by the government, in a trust. Each citizen would receive a one-acre home lot and a share of revenue from land sales and leases, and the trust would help develop a 60-square-mile free trade zone, where goods move without customs duties.

The first convention, on 23 February 1974, was addressed by John Hospers, the 1972 presidential candidate of the American Libertarian Party, who was later refused entry to the Bahamas. Around May 1974 reports appeared of a group of "20th Century Revolutionaries" and the movement denounced it. In February 1975 Esquire magazine reported that a rising was being planned, and the American arms dealer and mercenary Mitchell WerBell said Abaco would declare independence on its own. It was claimed that WerBell was managing and financing the movement and recruiting mercenaries.

No arrests followed, but the connection, which included visits to WerBell's Georgia estate, damaged the group. In March 1975 it renamed itself the Abaco Home Rule Movement, denied any military aims and published a draft constitution for an Abaco Commonwealth. In the 1977 general election the governing Progressive Liberal Party won 30 of 38 seats, including one on Abaco itself. That effectively ended the movement, and its newspaper stopped that year.

Abaco remains part of the Bahamas. The case shows the limits of a breakaway on an island where people already live under an elected government. Foreign money could print a newsletter and a constitution, but the plan needed local votes, and its ties to an arms dealer cost it support.

aerican-empire.story:
The Aerican Empire is a joke monarchy based in Montreal, Canada, founded on 8 May 1987 by Eric Lis, then a child, and a group of friends. It is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country that no government recognises. Its name plays on "American Empire", and its founders say it began as humour.

For its first ten years it was almost wholly fictional. It claimed a galaxy of invented planets and fought wars with other micronations that never involved physical contact. It went online in 1997, and in 2000 The New York Times called its site one of the more imaginative micronation sites.

Its activities are mostly games and jokes drawn from science fiction and fantasy, including story-writing contests, role-playing days and a Dog-Biscuit Appreciation Day scavenger hunt. It has a joke religion, the worship of the Great Penguin, which the group says has thirty followers. It describes itself as a parliamentary system with elected bodies under an emperor. It issued novelty passports from 2007, and one was shown that year at an art exhibition at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris. Its first stamps came in 2015. Its flag resembles Canada's, with a yellow smiling face in place of the red maple leaf.

Its mission statement says the Empire exists to help bring about a society in which the Empire is no longer needed. Lis, who went on to qualify as a physician at McGill University, remains Emperor, and in 2025 it hosted MicroCon in Montreal, attended by 120 people from 48 micronations.

No action by any government against it is known. It claims no real land from anyone, and it calls its passports novelties, so it poses no challenge to any state.

aeterna-lucia.story:
The Sovereign State of Aeterna Lucina, also called the Sovereign Humanitarian Mission State of Aeterna Lucina, was a self-declared country on private land in New South Wales, Australia. Paul Neuman, a German migrant, founded it in Byron Bay in 1978. He legally changed his name to Paul Baron Neuman and called himself the Supreme Lord. He said Hassan III, the exiled former king of Afghanistan, had made him Baron Neuman of Kara Bagh, and he claimed hundreds of other honours, including professorships and degrees in divinity.

The state had no fixed territory of its own and went wherever he did, first to Curl Curl in Sydney and then to Cooma. Its visible activity was the giving of titles. He sold at least one knighthood, reportedly for 1,900 Australian dollars to a man named Roland Bleyer.

It came to public attention in 1990, when he was charged with fraud in the New South Wales courts over land sales worth 144,000 Australian dollars. The case was dropped in 1992. His claim of sovereignty did not keep him out of court, since Australian law applied to him as to anyone else. The state lasted until his death, and sources give 1996 as its end. It is on the map as a claim to statehood that sat beside the sale of titles, with no effect on how Australian law treated the founder.

aigues-mortes.story:
The Principality of Aigues-Mortes is a humorous mock state in the walled town of Aigues-Mortes in southern France, started on 21 June 2010 as a parody of Monaco to attract media attention and tourists.

Its founders invented a story based on the town's real history. King Louis IX of France obtained the town in 1240 by swapping property with the monks who owned it. He sailed from there on two crusades, in 1248 and 1270, and died of dysentery in Tunis on the second. According to the invented tale, on his deathbed he made his loyal squire, Pierrot Pitchoun, Prince of Aigues-Mortes. The current prince is styled Sovereign-Prince Jean-Pierre IV, said to be the 22nd in this line.

The practical side is ordinary. The group is registered in France as an organisation called LOUPAM. With local merchants and the town's tourist office, it runs an exchange, the Bourse princière, for a local currency, the flamant, . It has attended micronation conferences in Perugia, Atlanta and Vincennes, and it hosted one in 2016.

No government recognises it, and the town remains part of France under French law. The case shows that a town can use the look of a state for promotion, and because it is open about the joke and works with local officials, nobody has a reason to object.

akhzivland.story:
Achzivland was a one-family micronation, a tiny self-declared country, on 1.4 hectares of the Mediterranean coast in northern Israel, near the Lebanese border. The site has a heavy history. It was a Palestinian fishing village known as al-Zeeb, whose residents fled when it was conquered in the 1948 war. A scholar who studied Achzivland, Philip Hayward, describes it as resting on ancestral Palestinian land, and says their forced removal is what made the place available.

Eli Avivi was born in Persia and came to British-ruled Palestine aged two. At 15 he joined a clandestine Jewish naval force and fought against the British and then Arab forces in 1948. He came across the site of Achziv in 1952 and settled among its ruined buildings, selling fish to a nearby kibbutz, a collective farm. He later married Rina.

The conflict with the state began in the 1960s, when the government decided to turn the area into a national park and sent bulldozers to destroy the buildings. Rina told the BBC that the army let him stay on condition that he worked as an undercover agent for Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency. Authorities then put up a fence that blocked the couple's way to the sea. They tore up their passports in protest and declared independence in 1971. They were briefly arrested, and the court case that followed made Achzivland internationally famous.

Daily life settled into a routine. The couple reached an agreement with the authorities to pay for access to the sea, and they opened a "national" museum of antiquities. Achzivland had a mermaid flag and its own passport, which asked that bearers be allowed to pass freely, and Avivi stamped visitors' passports as well. Hippies and celebrities came, including Sophia Loren.

Israel never recognised the place. The legal outcome was more ordinary than the flag suggests. A court leased the land to Avivi for 99 years, and a judge ruled that creating a country without permission was not an offence. A lease is a contract under Israeli law, so holding one meant accepting the state as landlord. In 2015 Avivi, then 85 and frail, told the BBC that the state did everything it could to get him out.

He died in May 2018, aged 88, leaving Rina as the only other citizen. She said she wanted the site to become a memorial to him. Ynet reported in January 2026 that she was still the site's one permanent resident. The case shows that a long-tolerated occupant can win the right to stay on while gaining no power to rule.

aramoana.story:
Aramoana is a small settlement on a sand spit at the mouth of Otago Harbour, about 20 km along the coast from Dunedin on New Zealand's South Island. It began in the 1880s as a pilot station for ships entering the harbour and later became a beach resort. The land was owned by the Otago Harbour Board and only leased to the people who lived there.

In the 1970s New Zealand's government wanted to reduce its dependence on selling wool and lamb to Britain. Prime Minister Robert Muldoon's "Think Big" program backed large industrial projects, and his National Development Act let the government push through projects of national importance with little regard for local objections. An aluminium smelter at Aramoana was one of them, proposed by a group of companies including Fletcher Challenge, CSR of Australia and Alusuisse of Switzerland. Many people in Dunedin wanted the jobs.

The Save Aramoana Campaign formed in 1974 to protect a wetland, the community and Māori burial sites. Local Māori leaders said they would not accept violation of the dead. Legal challenges failed, so the campaign turned to public opinion. It copied the non-violent tactics of the 1977 Māori occupation of Bastion Point, and artists including Ralph Hotere and poets including Cilla McQueen joined in. Eviction notices came anyway.

On 23 December 1980 residents declared the area independent of Otago and of New Zealand. The declaration was mainly a way to get attention and money. They produced flags, passports, stamps and a mock tax form to sell, and ran a travelling embassy. The fundraising is estimated to have brought in the equivalent of 500,000 dollars in 2022 money. A mock border post stood on the access road, ready in case construction vehicles appeared, and a campaign handbook told guards to ask newcomers whether they had any smelters concealed in their cars.

The fight was bitter locally. Businesses and artists who opposed the smelter sometimes had windows smashed, and Dunedin's mayor called opponents malcontents. In April 1981 the government confirmed residents would be evicted the following year. Then Alusuisse, which was to supply the technology, left the group. The government kept saying the project would continue, but nothing happened, and the later Labour government did not support it. The campaign itself credited a poor world aluminium market, its own pressure and public opinion, which stopped the government lowering the electricity price as far as it wanted.

The smelter was not built, Aramoana went back to being an ordinary part of New Zealand, and the nearby mudflats are now a wildlife sanctuary. The declaration had no legal force at any point. What it did was raise money and publicity for a campaign whose court cases had already failed.

atlantium.story:
The Empire of Atlantium is a micronation, a self-declared country that no government recognises, founded in Sydney, Australia, by three teenagers on 27 November 1981. George Cruickshank became head of state as Emperor George II, and Geoffrey Duggan served as prime minister from 1982 to 1986. By 1990 the original members had finished university and moved away, and the group went inactive.

In 1999 Cruickshank bought a 61-square-metre apartment in Potts Point, in inner Sydney, and revived it with a website, which brought in new members. Its capital had begun as a 10-square-metre plot in the suburb of Narwee. The apartment became the second capital. On 12 January 2008 a third was created in the Province of Aurora, 0.76 square kilometres of rural land about 350 km southwest of Sydney.

Atlantium calls itself primarily non-territorial, which means membership matters more than land. Almost 3,000 citizens were on its rolls in 2015, from over 100 countries, and most signed up online and never visited. It sold coins, stamps and banknotes in a currency called the imperial solidus, and it says the profits pay for operations and charity. It appointed unaccredited representatives in about ten countries, gave out honours and describes itself as promoting progressive, secular policies, so it works partly as a lobby group.

The group says its two properties have special status. In practice both stay under Australian law, and no country recognises it or has diplomatic relations with it. Owning land gives a person the rights of an owner and no more.

austenasia.story:
The Empire of Austenasia is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country, based in a suburban house in the London Borough of Sutton in England. Jonathan Austen, then a teenage student born in 1994, and his father Terry, a security guard turned gardener, founded it on 20 September 2008 by sending a declaration of independence for their house in Carshalton to their local Member of Parliament, Tom Brake. Terry became Emperor and Jonathan Prime Minister.

The first reply was silence. In May 2011 Jonathan met Brake, who asked Foreign Secretary William Hague what criteria Britain uses to recognise new states. Meanwhile Terry had stepped down in 2010, a successor had gone through a "civil war" and internal disputes, and a third leader held the post until January 2013, when Jonathan took the throne.

Jonathan began a program of growth, in which people around the world join by declaring their own home or a place they often visit part of the empire. It now claims dozens of properties, including houses in Britain, a holiday home in the Hebrides, part of a university campus in Australia, and places in the United States, Turkey and India. It claims to succeed the Roman Empire and has adopted Roman touches such as consuls and a senate, and Christianity was made its official religion in 2017. It sold commemorative coins for its tenth anniversary in 2018.

Jonathan stepped back in April 2024 and handed the running of it to a Prince Regent, Aggelos I. No government is known to recognise it, and the houses stay under the law of the countries they sit in, . Each declaration is a private statement by the owner and moves no border.

avram.story:
The Grand Duchy of Avram is a micronation in Tasmania, the island state of Australia, that claims no land and works mainly as a private bank issuing its own money. John Charlton Rudge, who had served one term as a Liberal Party member of the Tasmanian parliament, started it in the early 1980s and calls it "philosophical, not territorial". He styles himself Grand Duke and claims dozens of titles, including Earl of Enoch.

His Royal Bank of Avram opened in shops he owned in George Town and later moved to Strahan, on Tasmania's west coast. Customers exchanged Australian dollars for its banknotes and coins. They were linked to the value of gold, with 100 Ducals equal to one Avram and one Avram equal to a thirtieth of an ounce of gold.

In most countries a business needs a government licence to call itself a bank and take money, and Rudge had none. The Australian government seized his currency reserves and went to the Federal Court. Six cases followed, costing the federal government about 22 million Australian dollars. The courts found he had done nothing illegal and ordered the property returned, although some of it had disappeared in federal custody and later appeared for sale. Rudge resumed banking and issued more coins and notes, the most recent dated 2008. He told the press the bank worked from several unnamed sites, and its later activity is not known.

He later served as a councillor and deputy mayor of Sorell. The courts decided that he had broken no Australian law, and that gave the duchy no standing as a state.

bunte-republik-neustadt.story:
The Bunte Republik Neustadt, German for Colourful Republic of Neustadt, was a mock state in the Äußere Neustadt district of Dresden, in eastern Germany. In June 1990 East Germany still existed, with both East and West German marks in use around reunification, and the mock state made fun of its symbols.

It was proclaimed for a neighbourhood festival on 22 to 24 June 1990. Gregor Kunz, who became its first monarch, said the idea came up in conversation at a pub on Alaunstraße and was put together within two or three months. A provisional government formed, led by a "monarch without portfolio" and ministers with joke titles such as minister for "unculture and submarines". It issued decrees and demanded annexation by the Vatican.

A white line painted on the streets marked its borders, around a block of the district, with signs announcing the free territory. It created a currency, the Neustadtmark, with exchange booths offering one Neustadtmark for one East German mark or two for one West German mark. Its flag showed a Mickey Mouse head in a wreath of wheat, modelled on the East German coat of arms.

In 1993 the government dissolved itself by "going bathing" in the River Elbe, a joke about its pollution. The state ended there, and the festival went on each June, much less political. The city's conditions and violence between left- and right-wing groups defeated several attempts to run it through an organising body, with national headlines in 2001 and 2002 and twelve police officers injured in 2007. Since 2002 it has had no single organiser, and each person or bar registers its own event with the city. It ran yearly until 2019. German law applied throughout, and the city licensed and policed the events like any others.

capitol-hill-occupied-protest.story:
The Capitol Hill Occupied Protest, also called the Capitol Hill Organized Protest, CHOP or CHAZ, was a protest zone in the Capitol Hill neighbourhood of Seattle, Washington, in June 2020. It covered two intersections at the corners of Cal Anderson Park and the roads leading up to them, around the police department's East Precinct building, in a dense residential district.

In May 2020 a police officer in Minneapolis murdered George Floyd, and protests spread across the country. In Seattle, on 1 June police fired tear gas into the crowd at a rally downtown, and people moved to Capitol Hill, where police and protesters clashed every night. On 7 June a man drove toward the crowd near the precinct and shot a protester who tried to stop him. Police reported rocks, bottles and fireworks being thrown. Mayor Jenny Durkan's office told police to remove barricades, and on 8 June police boarded up and left the building. Who gave that order is disputed.

Protesters moved the barricades around the empty station and declared the area an autonomous zone, meaning one run by themselves. It had no official leaders, though some people named the rapper Raz Simone as one, which he denied. Decisions were made in daily assemblies. People ran free food, film screenings, medical stations and gardens. Its main demands were a 50 percent cut to police funding, with the money moved to programs in black communities, and no criminal charges for protesters.

Accounts varied from a block party to reports of intimidation by local businesses and residents. Police were not welcome inside. Shootings on 20, 21, 23 and 29 June killed two people and wounded others. After the last one, Durkan declared the gathering unlawful, and on 1 July police cleared it, after 23 days, arresting dozens.

The zone made no claim to be a country and sought no recognition. Washington state and Seattle law never stopped applying there. Police stayed out for three weeks, and that was a decision the city could reverse, as it did. Lawsuits followed, and the city later paid settlements including $10 million to protesters and $3.65 million to affected businesses.

conch-republic.story:
The Conch Republic is a joke country declared by the city of Key West, Florida, in protest against a federal roadblock. Key West sits at the far end of the Florida Keys, a chain of islands joined to the mainland by a single highway, US 1, and the town lives on tourism. In April 1982 the United States Border Patrol set up a checkpoint on that highway near Florida City, just where the Keys road meets the mainland, and stopped cars to search for drugs and illegal immigrants. Traffic backed up, and residents and tourists were badly delayed.

Key West's city council complained to the federal government repeatedly and got no answer. An attempt to win a court order against the roadblock failed. So on 23 April 1982 Mayor Dennis Wardlow and the council declared Key West independent, with Wardlow as prime minister. The new republic declared war on the United States by breaking a stale Cuban loaf over the head of a man in a naval uniform, surrendered to him after one minute, and applied for one billion dollars in foreign aid.

The event has been repeated every 23 April since then as a week-long festival. The name now covers all the Keys. The organisation calls itself a "sovereign state of mind" and works mainly as a tourism promoter. Representatives were invited to the 1994 Summit of the Americas in Miami and the 1995 Florida Jubilee.

It has kept using the joke to make real complaints. In September 1995 an Army Reserve unit planned an exercise on Key West simulating the invasion of a foreign island without telling local officials. The Conch "navy" attacked a Coast Guard cutter with water balloons and stale bread and protested to the Defense Department. During the federal government shutdown of 1995 and 1996, it sent boats to reopen Fort Jefferson in Dry Tortugas National Park with privately raised money. In 2006 it "annexed" an abandoned span of the Seven Mile Bridge after the government returned 15 Cuban refugees who had reached it, on the ground that the old bridge was not American soil.

Key West remains a Florida city, and no government has treated the declaration as a real one. The case shows a legal city government using a mock secession to publicise a complaint after a court case failed.

coral-sea-kingdom.story:
The Gay and Lesbian Kingdom of the Coral Sea Islands was a protest state on the Coral Sea Islands, small uninhabited islands and reefs east of the Great Barrier Reef. They form an external territory of Australia, created in 1969, spread over 780,000 square kilometres, most of it ocean. Miners dug guano there in the 1870s and 1880s, but the lack of fresh water stopped anyone staying.

The idea arose at the Brisbane Gay and Lesbian Pride Festival in 2003. In May 2004 the Australian government brought a bill to Parliament defining marriage as between a man and a woman, which also stopped same-sex couples married overseas from being recognised. Activists argued that the change had taken away equal rights and that they were owed compensation in territory, relying on the legal idea that what is unjustly taken must be paid back and on international statements about self-determination.

On 14 June 2004, after sailing on a ship named the Gayflower, a play on the Mayflower, activists led by Dale Parker Anderson raised the rainbow flag on Cato Island, the territory's highest point. They claimed the islands as a homeland for gay and lesbian people. A plaque there records the date, and a campsite called Heaven was named the capital. The declaration of independence borrowed from the American declaration and described a people who were still treated as strangers in their own countries. In a scheme modelled on Israel's Law of Return, which lets Jews settle in Israel, any gay or lesbian person could gain residence and citizenship. Anderson was elected administrator and then declared emperor, and the anthem was "I Am What I Am".

No one lived there. No challenge from the Australian government is known, and the islands stayed Australian. The scholar Judy Lattas of Macquarie University, who interviewed Anderson in 2007, treats it as a real secession and argues that gay nationalism may need territorial claims to secure rights. Others describe it as a symbolic protest.

Its leaders dissolved the kingdom on 17 November 2017, after the Yes result in Australia's postal survey on same-sex marriage. The campaign's goal was a change in Australian law, and its leaders ended the kingdom when that change was on its way.

crypto-valley-zug.story:
Crypto Valley is a nickname for Zug, a Swiss town of 30,934 people at the end of 2020, capital of the canton (state) of Zug and close to Zürich. Swiss cantons set many of their own taxes. From the second half of the 20th century Zug grew into a financial and trading centre by using low taxes to attract companies, and it is now headquarters to many multinationals.

Cryptocurrency firms followed the same route. Those based there include Ethereum, Cardano, Polkadot and Bitcoin Suisse. In 2016 the town began accepting digital currency for small fees up to 200 francs, converting it into Swiss francs straight away to reduce the risk of price swings. A Crypto Valley Association had formed by 2018, with Oliver Bussmann as president. The German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported in 2021 that taxes in the canton could be paid in Bitcoin.

People who want freedom from financial rules sometimes look at sea platforms or new countries. Zug is on the map as a different approach, which involves no claim to territory. Companies get low taxes and a welcoming local government, while Swiss courts and Swiss law still apply to them. Zug remains an ordinary part of Switzerland.

edge-esmeralda.story:
Edge Esmeralda is a month-long temporary village in Healdsburg, California, a town in Sonoma County about an hour north of San Francisco. People gather for several weeks and try out new ways of living, working and learning together. It is organised by a team called Edge City and described as a spin-off of Zuzalu, a similar gathering started by Vitalik Buterin of the cryptocurrency Ethereum. Gatherings of this kind are often called pop-up cities.

Its 2024 edition drew about 1,300 people, and the P2P Foundation calls it the first openly family-friendly village of this kind. The 2025 edition ran for four weeks and was built around themed weeks on subjects such as urban design, artificial intelligence, consciousness and health, with blood-testing labs and nightly saunas alongside talks. Nobody claims sovereignty, and the gathering takes place under ordinary law.

Its backers aim to build a permanent village, and this is where the law becomes concrete. The Esmeralda Land Company, associated with the organiser Devon Zuegel, has a concept for 266 acres at the southeast edge of Cloverdale, on an old lumber mill site directly beneath the runway approach of the Cloverdale Municipal Airport. California requires that development near airports fit safety zones meant to protect aircraft and people on the ground, and a proposal that does not conform cannot be approved. At a meeting in January 2026 the Sonoma County airport land use commission paused its review and asked for updated noise maps and limits on building near the runway. The developer described the materials as "a plan, a vision, a dialogue" and not yet a project.

Patch, a local news outlet, headlined the project as suspected of cyberlibertarian ties. Any village has to pass the same planning and safety reviews as other developments, and for this project the first obstacle was a county commission on airport safety.

federal-republic-of-montmartre-ny.story:
The Most Serene Federal Republic of Montmartre was a mock country claiming Manhattan's Theater District in New York City, from about 39th to 59th Street, with a strip up the Hudson River. Its founder and president was Barry Alan Richmond, a stage actor and director who wrote about the Grand Guignol, a form of horror theatre from the Montmartre district of Paris. He proclaimed it around 1965 and said it dated from a French colony founded in 1636 and cut off from France during the wars with Britain. He called it a "political fiction" and part of what he termed "total theater". It exchanged recognition with other micronations, offered asylum to almost anyone who asked, and claimed half of Kennedy Airport.

It came closest to official notice through the phone book. Richmond paid for a listing, "Montmartre Govt Of", in the blue government pages of the Manhattan directory. New York Telephone wanted it removed. On 24 June 1977 a hearing took place before the New York Public Service Commission, the state body that regulates utilities, in the World Trade Center. Richmond asked a federal court for an order to stop the removal and did not get one. An examiner ruled for the company on 30 June, and the commission set that ruling aside on 7 July. The company still printed 955,000 directories without the listing that August, and Richmond lost a court case to restore it in April 1978.

Mother Jones, the Los Angeles Times and New York Magazine covered the case. In December 1979 he announced that the commission had ruled for him and the listing would return, and a company spokesman complained that this was "simply not fair". The dispute was only ever about telephone rules. No regulator or court considered whether Montmartre was a country.

A 2001 Financial Times article found him still running it and trying to revive the Grand Guignol by selling his memorabilia collection. Nothing later is known about it.

fordlandia.story:
Fordlândia was a company town that the American carmaker Henry Ford built in the Amazon rainforest, on the Tapajós river in the state of Pará, Brazil, about 300 km south of Santarém. Cars need rubber for tyres. Ford wanted to reduce his reliance on European rubber makers, particularly after Winston Churchill proposed a rubber cartel.

Ford started it in 1928 on a land concession of about 10,000 square kilometres, meaning land the government let him use under agreed terms. He was exempted from taxes on goods exported from Brazil in exchange for 9 percent of profits, 7 percent for the national government and 2 percent for local towns. It was to house 10,000 people, and it looked like an American Midwestern town, with American-style houses, a hospital, a school, a swimming pool, a golf course and a cinema. Offices in Belém and Manaus recruited workers with promises of good wages.

Ford's managers ran daily life closely. Alcohol, tobacco and prostitution were forbidden, even in workers' own homes, and managers went from house to house checking. Workers paddled out to riverboats beyond the town's limits and hid drink inside watermelons, and a settlement of bars and brothels grew 5 miles upstream. Brazilian workers were fed brown rice, whole-wheat bread and oatmeal, as Ford believed proper, and they had to work through the midday heat.

The farming failed as well. The land was hilly and infertile, and none of the managers knew tropical agriculture. Wild rubber trees grow far apart as protection against pests, and these were planted close together, which made them easy prey for disease and insects.

In 1930 workers revolted in the cafeteria over the food and how it was served, an event known as the Quebra-Panelas, or Breaking Pans. They cut telegraph wires and drove managers into the jungle for days until the Brazilian Army arrived and ended it. Agreements were then made on the food. Brazil's government remained suspicious of foreign investment in the region and offered little help.

Ford Motor Company gave up on the town in 1934 and moved upriver to Belterra, where conditions were better. By 1945 synthetic rubber had removed the need, and Henry Ford II sold the land to the Brazilian government at a loss of over $20 million. It never produced rubber for Ford's tyres. About 90 residents remained until the 2000s, and about 3,000 people lived there by 2017.

Fordlândia never claimed to be a country. It is on the map as an example of a private ruler with vast land, his own town rules and almost unlimited money. Even so, his powers came from a contract with Brazil, the army that restored order was Brazil's, and the contract paid Brazil a share of the profits.

forvik.story:
Forvik was a state declared by one man on Forewick Holm, a one-hectare islet in the Sound of Papa in the Shetland Islands, north of mainland Scotland. Shetland has an unusual history. It was once ruled from Scandinavia. In 1469 King Christian I of Denmark and Norway, short of money, pawned his lands there to James III of Scotland for 8,000 florins, and Scotland and later Britain have governed the islands ever since.

Stuart Hill, from Essex in England, was shipwrecked on the islet in 2001 during a failed trip around Britain, which earned him the nickname Captain Calamity. He settled in Shetland and took up that history. He argues that James received only Christian's land, held in trust and only until the debt was paid, and that the islands were never formally handed to Scotland or Britain, so British rule there has no legal basis. Few Shetlanders showed interest.

To draw attention, he acquired the islet and on 21 June 2008 declared it Forvik, a dependency of the British Crown outside the United Kingdom and the European Union. He invited Shetlanders to add their own property. On 23 February 2011 he went further and declared it a fully independent Sovereign State. His ownership is itself disputed. The former owner, Mark King, says he signed the donation document during a manic episode and that the land registry still lists him as owner. Hill began building a residence, offered oil companies rights to the seabed and sold citizenship for 60 to 360 pounds, later replaced by a membership of 20 pounds a year, with 218 members claimed in 2015. In September 2008 a Coastguard helicopter and lifeboat had to rescue him when his plywood boat began to sink. He stopped paying value-added tax and built without planning permission, and no charges followed from those. In 2010 he helped launch a Sovereign Nation of Shetland.

The test came through his vans. In 2011, aged 68, he was charged with 12 motoring offences, including having no insurance, tax, licence or vehicle safety certificate, on vans he said were consular vehicles for Forvik. At Lerwick Sheriff Court (a sheriff is a Scottish judge) he was locked up for 20 minutes after refusing to answer the charges. He then presented a 71-page argument that the court had no power in Shetland. This is a question of jurisdiction, meaning a court's power to decide a case. Sheriff Graeme Napier heard it over two days, called Hill deluded and seriously misguided, and dismissed it. In December 2011 Hill was found guilty on six charges, fined £1,400, and given 100 hours of unpaid work and a six-month driving ban.

He kept campaigning, and in December 2025, aged 82, he was again found guilty of driving offences after another sheriff rejected the same argument.

For anyone relying on an old document, the case shows what happens in practice. The Scottish court held that the historical argument gave no defence to ordinary driving charges. The authorities brought no charges over the tax or the building, and the claim was tested when he was charged with motoring offences.

free-republic-of-wendland.story:
The Free Republic of Wendland was a protest camp near Gorleben in northern West Germany, set up to stop a planned nuclear waste site. Nuclear power stations produce waste that stays dangerous for a very long time, and governments look for places to bury it deep underground. In 1979 a federal agency drilled at Gorleben to test whether the salt domes there were suitable. Small occupations at two drilling sites failed, so activists planned a larger one that would bring in anti-nuclear activists from other countries.

On 3 May 1980 about 5,000 people moved onto the area around drilling site 1004, on sandy ground burned by a forest fire in 1975, and proclaimed a republic. The state interior minister, Egbert Möcklinghoff, called the proclamation high treason.

About 1,000 people stayed permanently, for 33 days. In a few days they built about 110 huts of wood and clay, a Friendship House holding 100 people, greenhouses, an infirmary, a hairdresser and a sauna, with water from a wind-powered well warmed by solar power. A checkpoint with a barrier marked the entrance. Their information centre sold a passport called the Wendenpass for 10 marks, said to be valid for the entire universe so long as its owner could still laugh. Decisions were made at mass meetings through a council of spokespeople, and most agreed on passive resistance if police came. Local people brought food and timber. Thousands visited at weekends, among them the future chancellor Gerhard Schröder. Radio Free Wendland began pirate broadcasts, meaning unlicensed radio, on 18 May.

On 4 June, on Chancellor Helmut Schmidt's orders, about 3,500 police and federal border guards cleared the camp. About 2,000 occupiers held a sit-in in the central square, and many were carried away. The clearance was largely peaceful, and the police thanked the crowd over a loudspeaker for staying non-violent. The legal grounds were ordinary ones, including forestry law, building regulations and registration law. Nothing in the clearance depended on the claim of statehood.

A 30th anniversary gathering in 2010 drew about 800 people. The declaration had no legal effect, and the camp lasted until the government decided to clear it.

frestonia.story:
Frestonia was a mock independent state set up by squatters on Freston Road in Notting Dale, west London, to stop their homes being demolished. Squatting means living in an empty building without the owner's permission. In the 1970s rented flats in London were scarce and often in slum condition, and council housing lists served families and ran for years. Many Victorian cottages on Freston Road had been condemned as unfit to live in, and their residents had been moved to new tower blocks. The authorities left the empty houses standing because neighbours complained that clearing them would leave rubble and dumping.

Squatters moved in from 1974. They included the photographer Tony Sleep, who recalled one candlelit room with no toilet, water or electricity on his first visit, and then friends fitting plumbing and wiring. People shared little beyond needing somewhere to live, and some houses were quickly wrecked.

When the Greater London Council, the city's government, planned to clear the 1.8-acre site, the 120 residents all took the surname Bramley so the council would have to rehouse them together as one family. The council then threatened eviction. At a public meeting of 200 people, resident Nicholas Albery suggested seceding, inspired by the film Passport to Pimlico and a visit to Christiania in Copenhagen. A referendum showed 94 percent in favour.

They declared independence on 31 October 1977, applied to the United Nations and warned that peacekeeping troops might be needed. The actor David Rappaport became foreign minister, the playwright Heathcote Williams ambassador to Britain, and a two-year-old child education minister. They issued stamps and visas and designed a flag. Sleep later called it "part publicity stunt, part theatrical protest", and said it was not a serious attempt to leave the UK. Shadow Chancellor Geoffrey Howe sent a supportive letter, and Williams won a court ruling that, for a dispute over his play The Immortalist, the area was not part of the United Kingdom.

The publicity is what mattered. The Daily Mirror and other papers covered the community, and that made demolition harder. By 1982 the council had dropped it. There were then 23 houses and 97 residents, who formed a housing co-operative and negotiated with the Notting Hill Housing Trust, a housing charity.

The co-operative still manages homes on the site, a Frestonian Gallery keeps the name, and the community no longer claims independence. The case shows a mock secession working as a bargaining tactic. The residents won under ordinary law, through a housing co-operative.

ganienkeh.story:
Ganienkeh, meaning Land of the Flint in Mohawk, is a community of traditionalist Mohawks on land near Altona in the far northeast corner of New York State, about 12 miles from the Canadian border. The Mohawk are one of the nations of the Iroquois Confederacy, whose territory once covered much of the region. Residents call it an independent North American Indian state.

The land claim goes back to the American Revolution. The Iroquois had sided with the defeated British and were forced to give up land to New York afterward. The founders of Ganienkeh argued that a 1797 deal between New York and the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant was a fraud that could not cancel Mohawk rights. They had also left reservations such as Akwesasne and Kahnawake to rebuild a traditional life away from alcohol and drug problems.

In May 1974 a group occupied Moss Lake, a girls' camp near Old Forge, New York, and sent a manifesto, compiled by Louis Karoniaktajeh Hall, to the United Nations and President Nixon. The armed occupation lasted three years and ended in 1977 after nearly 200 negotiating sessions. The group agreed to move to land at Miner Lake that the state had planned as a park. Mario Cuomo, then acting for New York State, set up a body called the Turtle Island Trust to hold the lease, which at first covered about 5,700 acres.

This settled the occupation and left the principle open. On the state's ten recognised reservations, tribes deal with the federal government and the state has no authority over them. At Ganienkeh the relationship with New York has never been defined. Local residents sued to void the lease, and the state's top court upheld it in 1981. It expired in 1992 and has run month to month since.

The first winter was hard. People had been allowed to bring only their personal property, they had no electricity or running water, and local townspeople helped with food. Buildings used materials from Moss Lake. The group hoped to live without money, but income from tax-free cigarettes paid for development. Tax-free bingo came in 1990, with a 1,500-seat hall, followed by a golf course and an unlicensed casino that has drawn complaints. Businesses are run communally, every resident may take part in community meetings, alcohol and recreational drugs are banned, and a school teaches Mohawk. The community relies on the Two Row Wampum, which it says guarantees its right to exist as a sovereign people. Its flag, designed by Hall, later became a symbol in the 1990 Oka Crisis in Quebec.

In 1990 a rifle shot traced to the area wounded a doctor on a Vermont National Guard helicopter. When state police came to investigate, an 11-day armed standoff followed, with no arrests. Clinton County auctioned 11 of the trust's land parcels in 2012 over about $300,000 in back taxes, and a ruling favoured the county, with a final ruling in 2025.

The community continues to live there on those terms. The case shows a people who gained real land and a large measure of practical independence through armed occupation and long negotiation, while the state kept its position that its courts and tax collectors can reach land held through a trust.

glacier-republic.story:
The Glacier Republic is a mock state that the environmental group Greenpeace declared over Chile's glaciers on 5 March 2014, to push Chile into passing a law protecting them. Chile holds 82 percent of South America's glaciers. Greenpeace objected to mining companies building on or near them.

Its argument used the language of international law. Matías Asún, head of Greenpeace in Chile, said neither the constitution nor the water code names glaciers as a public good that must be protected, and Chile had no specific glacier law. So, the group said, there was a legal vacuum that let it found a country there, and it also pointed to unclear points in the border between Chile and Argentina. It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times. More than 40,000 people signed up as citizens within ten days, and it named embassies in about 40 countries, essentially the places where Greenpeace already had offices.

Greenpeace said the republic would hand the glaciers back to Chile once a suitable law passed. The legal gap may be narrower than claimed. The Civil Code makes all waters national public goods, and the Basic Environmental Law lists glaciers among protected areas, and Chile's government treats the glaciers as within its territory.

Six deputies introduced a glacier bill in 2014, and it was still being debated in late 2015. Whether a law has since passed is not known. The republic works as advertising with a legal argument attached, and Greenpeace itself presents it as temporary.

goust.story:
Goust is a hamlet of about one square mile (2.5 square kilometres) on a plateau at 995 metres in the Western Pyrenees of southwestern France. It can be reached only by a narrow footpath across a bridge called the Pont d'Enfer, or Bridge of Hell. It has 10 to 12 households and between 50 and 150 people, who lived traditionally from animals, wool and silk and more recently from tourism. It belongs to Laruns, a French commune (local municipality) in the valley below.

Writers in the 19th century described Goust as an independent republic, and it is on the map because that story keeps being repeated. The idea goes back to an 1827 description by Joseph Lainé, a former French interior minister. In 1858 another writer, Jean-François Samazeuilh, said Lainé had been speaking in metaphor and that later authors had taken him literally.

The evidence against independence is everyday. Residents paid their taxes to the government in Laruns and went to the church there for baptisms, weddings and burials.
