Because of the terrain, coffins were sent down the mountainside on a chute to be collected for burial at Laruns. American newspapers reported an uprising in 1896 over a ban on newspapers, but that report has never been verified.

Goust's independence is treated today as folklore, and the hamlet is an ordinary part of France. Being described as independent in print did not change who collected the tax.

holy-empire-of-reunion.story:
The Holy Empire of Reunion is an invented country created on 28 August 1997 by law students at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It claims Réunion, an island of about 2,511 square kilometres in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department of France, meaning a full administrative part of the French state.

The founders were on another continent, so nobody moved anywhere. The project has been described as a parody of the French department and as a simulation for practising politics and constitutional law, . A Brazilian newspaper covered it in 1998 when it moved onto the internet.

It is not known to have tried to take control of the island or to have drawn any response from France, and whether the project is still active is not known. It is on the map as a claim on land already inhabited and governed, made from abroad as a study exercise.

hutt-river.story:
The Principality of Hutt River was a farm in Western Australia, 517 kilometres north of Perth near the town of Northampton, whose owner declared it an independent country. It lasted 50 years as a micronation. A micronation is a tiny self-declared country that no government recognises.

It began with wheat. Leonard Casley, a farmer, had about 4,000 hectares of crop ready to harvest when new state government quotas allowed him to sell only about 40 hectares' worth. Five families who farmed at Hutt River banded together, and Casley protested to the governor of Western Australia, without result. He says a bill was then introduced to take the families' land under compulsory purchase laws. On 21 April 1970 he declared his 75-square-kilometre farm the independent Hutt River Province, saying that international law allowed it, while also saying he stayed loyal to Queen Elizabeth II.

He built his case from legal fragments. A letter from the governor-general's office once addressed him as "Administrator of the Hutt River Province", and he treated that as recognition. He began calling himself Prince Leonard because he believed a 1495 English law protected a ruling king from treason charges. He also believed the federal government had two years to respond to his declaration, and he said its silence gave him self-rule in practice from 21 April 1972. Australian courts did not accept these arguments.

The farm became a regional tourist attraction, and Casley said he kept selling wheat in defiance of the quota. He issued a currency, more than 50 sets of stamps and passports, none of which any government accepted. Visitors got entry visas, and an anthem was written in 1984.

Australia still expected him to pay tax. In February 1977 he was convicted for failing to give tax documents to the Australian Taxation Office. That December he declared war on Australia and ended the war days later, apparently on the theory that a government must respect an undefeated nation under the Geneva Conventions. In 1978 he lost an appeal over running a shop without a permit. When others sued him over a land deal and a printing bill, he did not claim to be beyond the courts' reach. Around 2006 he lost again to the tax office, and the High Court of Australia dismissed his application as fatuous, frivolous and vexatious, a phrase for a case with no legal merit. In June 2017 a judge of the Supreme Court of Western Australia rejected the argument that the court had no power over Hutt River and ordered Leonard to pay A$2.7 million and his son Arthur A$242,000 in unpaid tax.

Leonard handed over to his youngest son, Graeme, in 2017 and died in February 2019, leaving a tax debt of about A$2.5 million. In December 2019, citing lower farm income and fewer tourists, the principality said it would close to visitors from the end of January 2020. On 3 August 2020 Graeme dissolved it, citing hard times in the pandemic, and the farm went on sale.

For decades Australia left the farm alone, apart from the tax cases. Its courts treated the Casleys as Australian taxpayers throughout, and the debt passed to the founder's son.

islandia.story:
The Principality of Islandia is a micronation, meaning a self-declared country that no government recognises, on Coffee Caye, a mangrove-covered island of about half a hectare in the Caribbean Sea, a short boat trip from Belize City and surrounded by coral reefs. Gareth Johnson and Marshall Mayer founded it in February 2018. It was the first attempt at a micronation paid for by crowdfunding, in which many people each contribute money, here to buy an island.

It has about 250 citizens, none of whom live on the island, which can be rented for camping trips. A 2024 article reported plans to elect a new head of state. The island remains part of Belize. Crowdfunding can pay for land, and the question of who governs that land stays with Belize.

jamtland-republic.story:
The Republic of Jämtland, in full the United Republics of Jämtland, Härjedalen and Ravund, is a humorous cultural and marketing project in the Jämtland region of central Sweden. It began in 1963 and 1964 as a reaction to two things, people moving away from the county and a plan by the central government to merge Jämtland County with neighbouring Västernorrland. Its founders formed a Liberation Movement and gathered support through Storsjöyran, a local "freedom festival" in Östersund.

The joke rests on a real history. From the 10th to the 12th century Jämtland governed itself and answered to no crown. The Norwegian crown annexed it in 1178, and even then it kept much self-rule and connected to the king mainly through taxes. It is part of Sweden today. The movement proclaimed a republic "within the Kingdom of Sweden", which signals that it is not a real attempt to leave.

Its presidents have been entertainers, starting with the television performer Yngve Gamlin in 1963. The comedian Moltas Erikson, president from 1983 to 1988, called the movement 51 percent jest and 49 percent earnest. Ewert Ljusberg used a yearly festival speech to mock the Swedish government and the European Union, and the actress Eva Röse has held the post since 2022. The republic has a blue, white and green flag, popular locally though with no legal status, and an anthem in Swedish and Jamtlandic.

Local support for real independence is low, and the movement mainly works to preserve Jämtlandic culture and language. The area remains part of Sweden. The case shows a region using an old history of self-rule to promote its culture and needle the capital.

kalakuta-republic.story:
The Kalakuta Republic was the home compound of the Nigerian musician and activist Fela Kuti at 14 Agege Motor Road, in the Mushin area of Lagos, Nigeria. Nigeria was then ruled by the military. After returning from the United States in 1970, Kuti declared the compound independent of the state. The name mocked a prison cell called Calcutta in which he had been held, itself named after the Black Hole of Calcutta. The compound housed his family and band, a recording studio and a free health clinic.

Kuti's music attacked the government openly. His record Zombie compared soldiers to zombies who obey orders blindly, and it was popular in Nigeria and angered the head of state, General Olusegun Obasanjo. The military said it was unseemly to have a republic within a republic.

On 18 February 1977 about a thousand armed soldiers attacked, and the compound burned to the ground. Kuti's mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a second-floor window and died after about eight weeks in a coma. The next year Kuti married 27 of his singers, who he said could not find work after the studio was burned and needed protection.

The site was later rebuilt, in an effort led by Governor Babatunde Fashola, and it opened as the Kalakuta Republic Museum on 15 October 2012, with his clothes, instruments and art, a restaurant and a hotel. No court ever considered the claim of independence. It was a political gesture against a military government, and that government answered with soldiers.

keraton-agung-sejagat.story:
Keraton Agung Sejagat, meaning Universal Grand Throne, was a mystical movement and invented kingdom based in Purworejo Regency, Central Java, Indonesia. Its founders, Totok Santoso Hadiningrat and Dyah Gitarja, began it in 2018 and gathered around 450 members.

Hadiningrat had tried a similar scheme before. In 2016 he founded the Jogjakarta Development Committee, promising members payments of 100 to 200 dollars a month from an account at a fictional Swiss bank. The money never came. This time he used history. He said a ruler of the old Majapahit Empire, a real kingdom in Java, had handed sovereignty, meaning supreme authority, to the Portuguese in 1518 on condition that it be returned after 500 years. Since those 500 years ended in 2018, he claimed authority over every country on Earth, with the United Nations as his legislature, the International Court of Justice as his judiciary and the Pentagon as his defence department. Members paid about 200 dollars each for uniforms and titles.

On 12 January 2020 the group held a public ritual in Pogung Juru Tengah township, and residents who were uneasy about it complained to the police. Officers came the next day, arrested the two founders on 14 January and named them suspects on the 15th. On 21 January Hadiningrat told a press conference that the kingdom was a scam and its history was made up. A University of Indonesia historian, Bondan Kanumoyoso, pointed out that the Majapahit Empire had collapsed in 1478, before the supposed treaty.

How any case against them ended is not known. The group claimed the whole world, and neighbours' complaints to the police ended it within days.

killington-new-hampshire.story:
Killington is a ski resort town of 1,407 people (2020 census) in Rutland County, Vermont, in the northeastern United States. Its voters have twice approved the idea of leaving Vermont to join New Hampshire, a state 25 miles to the east.

The cause was school funding. In 1997, under a state Supreme Court order, Vermont adopted a system for paying for schools that sharply raised property taxes in towns with valuable property such as Killington, which has a ski resort and many vacation lodges. Some residents felt the taxes they sent to the state were out of line with the services they received. They also pointed out that the town was first chartered by New Hampshire on 7 July 1761.

The first vote came at a town meeting in March 2004, in an elementary school, by voice, with officials estimating that about two-thirds of the 200 to 300 people present were in favour. "It is Killington's obligation to break that ground," one resident, Jim Blackman, said. The town had spent about $20,000 studying the move. New Hampshire's governor, Craig Benson, said he did not think it would happen.

The votes were largely symbolic, because a town cannot leave on its own. Moving it would need approval from both state legislatures and the United States Congress, since it changes the borders of two states. Killington remains a town in Vermont.

kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.story:
The Kingdom of Araucania and Patagonia was a state proclaimed in 1860 by a French lawyer over the lands of the Mapuche, an Indigenous people, in what is now southern Chile and Argentina. The Mapuche lived south of the Biobío River, and their leaders wanted to stay independent of the Chilean and Argentine governments.

Antoine de Tounens, a former lawyer from Périgueux in France, decided to go there after reading La Araucana, an epic poem about the region, and hoped to be its king. He reached Chile in 1858 and met Mapuche leaders, promising guns and French help to keep them independent. Some leaders, including Kilapan and Kalfukura, backed him and chose him as a supreme chief, possibly because they believed a European could help their cause.

In November 1860 he issued two decrees saying that Araucania and eastern Patagonia belonged to no other state and naming himself King Orelie-Antoine I, with a hereditary constitutional government. He named Perquenco his capital, created a flag and had coins minted under the name Nouvelle France. He wrote later of his reasoning, asking whether the Araucanians were not free to give him power and he to accept it.

Chile answered with force. President José Joaquín Pérez authorised his arrest, which came on 5 January 1862. A court in Santiago declared him insane on 2 September, and in October he was expelled to France. He tried three more times to return, and each time he was captured and sent back. In 1870 the Chilean commander Saavedra suspected French interference, and there were reports that arms seized in Buenos Aires in 1871 had been ordered by Tounens. In 1873 a court in Paris ruled that he had not justified his claim to be a sovereign. He died in poverty in Tourtoirac, France, on 17 September 1878, and his death has been attributed to ill health from captivity.

His declaration has been described as one cause of the Chilean occupation of Araucania, in which the state took the Mapuche lands. The Mapuche leaders had backed him in hope of staying independent, and that is not what followed. Historians Simon Collier and William Sater call the kingdom a "curious and semi-comic episode". The case shows that a proclamation by a foreigner did not stop a neighbouring state from arresting him, and that such a claim can give that state a further reason to move.

kingdom-of-elleore.story:
Elleore is a small island of about 15,000 square metres in Roskilde Fjord, an inlet on the Danish island of Zealand, north of the town of Roskilde. It is run as a mock kingdom by the people who own it. Before 1944 it was known mainly as the place where a controversial 1907 film, Løvejagten, was shot.

In 1944, during the German occupation of Denmark, a group of Copenhagen schoolteachers bought it for a summer camp. They declared it a kingdom as a gentle parody of Denmark's government and royal traditions, and gave it an invented history going back to Irish monks in the 10th century.

Its place names, government bodies and noble titles imitate the Danish ones. It bans the novel Robinson Crusoe and keeps Elleore Standard Time, 12 minutes behind Danish time. It has issued stamps and coins. The island is empty except for a week-long gathering each year called the Elleuge, attended by dozens of citizens, when the monarch is enthroned. The capital, Maglelille, is a town of tents that exists only during that week.

Because the founders own the island, the project has had no conflict with the Danish state, and it continues today. Private ownership gives them control over how the land is used, and Denmark keeps its sovereignty, the supreme power to govern.

kingdom-of-lovely.story:
The Kingdom of Lovely was a joke country created for How to Start Your Own Country, a six-part British comedy documentary shown in August and September 2005. The presenter, the comedian Danny Wallace, set out to see what founding a country really takes.

He visited Sealand, a claimed state on an old fort off England, and met a man who claims to own the Moon. He "invaded" Eel Pie Island in the Thames and left when police were called. He then settled on his flat in Bow, east London, as territory, proclaimed himself king and sent a declaration of independence to the Prime Minister. Along the way he chose a flag and anthem, designed a currency called the IOU and showed it to Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England's chief cashier, applied for foreign aid, and tried to enter the Eurovision Song Contest.

The project ran partly on the internet, and at its peak 58,165 people registered as citizens on its website, citizensrequired.com, which is no longer active. In the last episode he went to New York to seek support at the United Nations, and the lack of real territory let him down. A final gathering of citizens took place in Leicester Square, where he revealed the country's name.

Its claimed dates run from 1 January 2005 to 19 May 2013, and no state recognised it. The flat stayed under British law, and the series ended with no state having accepted the claim.

kingdom-of-redonda.story:
Redonda is an uninhabited rock just over a mile long and a third of a mile wide, rising to 296 metres, between Nevis and Montserrat in the Caribbean. It is part of the country of Antigua and Barbuda. It has no fresh water apart from rain, it is steep on nearly every side, and boats can land only in calm seas on the sheltered coast. From 1865 to 1912 it was mined for guano, seabird droppings used as fertiliser, with many thousands of tons of phosphate shipped to Britain. Ruins of the mine remain.

The kingdom is a literary joke. The writer M.P. Shiel, an author of adventure and fantasy novels, first told the story in 1929 in a pamphlet promoting a reissue of his books. He claimed that his father, a trader from Montserrat, founded a Kingdom of Redonda in 1865, and that he himself was crowned there in 1880. No independent evidence supports this, though an oral memory of the coronation exists on Montserrat. In 1936 Shiel passed the title and the rights to his work to the London poet John Gawsworth, who held court as King Juan in a Bayswater pub, handed out titles to literary friends and is said to have given the throne away several times when short of money.

It later went to the publisher Jon Wynne-Tyson, who gave it up in 1997 in favour of the Spanish novelist Javier Marías. Marías died in 2022, and the writer Juan Gabriel Vásquez, reported as his successor, has said no official naming took place. Rival claimants still dispute the title half-seriously.

The government acted without reference to any of them. From 2016 goats and rats were removed from the island, and the vegetation returned. In September 2023 the country created the Redonda Ecosystem Reserve across nearly 30,000 hectares of land and sea, the largest marine protected area in the region.

Antigua and Barbuda has never contested the literary kingdom. The title passes among writers, and the island is governed by the state that created the reserve.

kingdom-of-romkerhall.story:
Romkerhall is a hotel and restaurant on the River Oker in the Harz Mountains of Germany, opposite an artificial waterfall about 64 metres high, and it advertises itself as a kingdom. It lies about 5 kilometres south of the village of Oker. An innkeeper named Lüer opened the first house here on 1 May 1863 on land leased from the Brunswick forestry office, and he created the waterfall that same year to draw visitors.

Since 1988 the restaurant's managers have promoted the place as the "Kingdom of Romkerhall, the smallest kingdom in the world". They base this on a real feature of German local government, because the property belongs to no municipality and sits in an unincorporated area of Goslar county in Lower Saxony. An unincorporated area has no town council of its own, but it remains part of its county, its state and Germany. The title is still used to market the hotel and waterfall.

kingdom-of-sedang.story:
The Kingdom of Sedang was a state declared in 1888 by a French adventurer among the hill peoples of what is now central Vietnam. In the 1880s France held French Indochina and protected the emperor of Annam, and Siam, now Thailand, was claiming land near French holdings.

Charles-Marie David de Mayrena was a former French official, allegedly involved in embezzlement, who owned a plantation in the colony. When Siam's claims worried a colonial official, he convinced that official to send him inland to negotiate treaties with local peoples for France.

On arrival he persuaded the chiefs to form a kingdom under him instead. He argued that the tribes were not subjects of the emperor of Annam, and so were entitled to independence. The chiefs of the Bahnar, Rengao and Sedang elected him, and on 3 June 1888 he took the title Marie the First, with his capital at the village of Kon Gung.

The rest of the story took place far from the highlands. He offered to hand his kingdom to France in return for a trade monopoly and hinted that Prussia was interested. France did not respond positively, and Britain turned him away in Hong Kong. In Belgium in 1889 a financier offered weapons and money in exchange for mineral rights. He handed out dozens of noble titles and medals and printed postage stamps, which are the main thing the kingdom left behind. The French Navy then blockaded Vietnamese ports and seized his arms in Singapore as contraband, so he could not return.

He died on 11 November 1890 on the island of Tioman in Malaya, with reports blaming poison, a snakebite or a duel, and the kingdom ended with him. The case shows that an election by local chiefs did not make a state when a colonial power controlled the ports and refused recognition. His weapons and money could not reach the kingdom.

kingdom-of-tavolara.story:
Tavolara is an island off the northeast coast of Sardinia, in Italy, whose Bertoleoni family claims it as one of the world's smallest kingdoms. The island was uninhabited when Joachim Murat visited in 1815. The Bertoleoni family says King Charles Albert of Sardinia approved its title. The claim is dated to 1836, when Giuseppe Bertoleoni was head of the family. Giuseppe's son became King Paolo I in the 1840s and reigned until 1886.

What is known is how Italy behaved. In 1861 it paid 12,000 lire for land at the island's northeast end to build a lighthouse, which began operating in 1868. That is how a government acts toward an owner under its own law.

After Paolo's death in 1886 newspapers reported that the island had become a republic under his will. The New York Times described a president and a council of six, elected every six years by men and women alike and supposedly recognised by Italy in 1887. This has not been confirmed, and the family's line went on. Carlo I died in 1928, and his son Paolo II went abroad. Paolo's aunt Mariangela ruled as regent, or stand-in, until her death in 1934, which is said to have left the kingdom to Italy. Paolo II kept claiming it until he died in 1962, the year a NATO military station was installed on the island.

Tonino Bertoleoni, the head of the family, runs a restaurant called Da Tonino on the island, and Paolo I's tomb in the graveyard has a crown on top. The family keeps up the claim. It has never stopped the Italian state from using the island.

kingdom-of-wallachia.story:
The Kingdom of Wallachia is a joke kingdom and tourism venture in Moravian Wallachia, a region in the southeast of the Czech Republic. The photographer Tomáš Harabiš founded it in 1997 as what he called an elaborate practical joke, and the actor Bolek Polívka was appointed King Boleslav I, with a lavish coronation in 2000. A reported 80,000 Czech citizens have acquired its passports.

The joke became a real money dispute. In 2001 the "Wallachian government", meaning Harabiš, removed Polívka, accusing him of demanding one million Czech koruna for his services. Polívka said he had been king since proclaiming it on a television show in 1993 and that 23 of the kingdom's 28 municipalities still recognised him.

Because the two could not settle it, the case went to court in Ostrava in 2007. A trademark is a legal right to a name used in business, and that was the real issue. The court ruled for Harabiš, rejecting Polívka's claim to own the "Kingdom of Wallachia" trademark and barring him from profiting from it, and a court ruled the same way in 2008. A tournament then chose a new king, Vladimír Zháněl, as Vladimír II.

The kingdom has no diplomatic recognition and continues as a tourist attraction. When its two rulers fell out, the only government that could decide between them was the Czech Republic.

kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.story:
Kiribati is a Pacific nation of low coral islands called atolls, with little soil. Nearly all its vegetables are imported. This is a purchase of farmland in Fiji by Kiribati's government, made with climate change in mind.

In May 2014 President Anote Tong said the government had made the final payment of 8.6 million American dollars for the Natoavatu Estate on Vanua Levu, one of Fiji's islands. The 2,210-hectare property, about 22 square kilometres, had belonged to the Anglican church and had once been a cattle and copra ranch worked by labourers from the Solomon Islands. It lies at the end of a dirt road about 55 km from the town of Savusavu, and about half of it is thick jungle. The money came from Kiribati's national savings fund of nearly A$1 billion. It was bought without review by Kiribati's parliament, for about four times the average price per acre of comparable land.

Tong described it as helping Kiribati's economic and food security as the climate changed. His environment minister said at the time that they were looking for a place that could hold 60,000 or 70,000 people. Scientists disputed the reasoning, saying sand atolls can rise with the sea.

Tong's successor, Taneti Maamau, took a different line. In February 2021 he announced that the land would return to being a commercial farm to feed Kiribati, with technical help from China. His government had switched its diplomatic ties from Taiwan to Beijing in 2019, so the news set off rumours that the land would pass to China. His office called those rumours a fabrication, and he ruled out any military use, saying China would only provide technical advice. Opponents asked him to be open about the plan, including who would farm it and for whom.

The law on this is plain. Buying land in another country gets a government the same thing it gets a private buyer, a title. Fiji remains the governing state, its law applies on the estate, and Kiribati holds it as an ordinary owner. So a nation that lost its land would still need the host country's agreement to move people there, .

laas-en-bearn.story:
Laàs is a village of 135 people in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques area of southwest France, between Bayonne and Pau. It declared itself a principality on 1 January 2015. The mayor, Jacques Pédéhonta, first floated the idea in August 2011 in protest against government reforms of local government, and the village opposed the NOTRe law, a national reform meant to cut administrative costs . A list of micronations describes the move as a secession over neglect by the national government, while the mayor described it as a shared dream to support the local economy.

The mayor was open about how it worked. He told Sud Radio in 2018 that the village was not really a principality but acted as if it were. The legal basis is an ordinary association, registered as a non-profit with the prefecture in Pau in May 2014. The village adopted a constitution, a coat of arms and a motto, and placed a customs booth at its entrance, all without the consent of the French presidency, as he noted.

Visitors can buy a day in the principality. They cross customs, visit the château, walk a boulevard of stars in imitation of Hollywood and eat at the village inn. It received 28 buses in 2018, and a shop for local products and a passport were planned. Laàs is still a French commune with a French mayor, and the project shows a small place using a mock state as a tourism plan.

ladonia.story:
Ladonia is a declared country covering the area around large sculptures in the Kullaberg nature reserve in northwest Skåne, southern Sweden. In 1980 the Swedish artist Lars Vilks began building them there. Nimis, Latin for "too much", is made of 75 tonnes of driftwood. Arx, Latin for "fortress", is made of stone. The spot is so hard to reach that nobody found them for two years. The local council then ruled that they were buildings, which were forbidden on the reserve, and ordered them removed.

Vilks appealed repeatedly and lost, and the Swedish government finally settled the matter in the council's favour. Meanwhile the work changed hands. The artist Joseph Beuys bought Nimis in 1984, and after his death the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude bought it. Many local people, especially in tourism, supported the sculptures.

On 2 June 1996, in protest against the council, Vilks declared the area an independent country called Ladonia. In 1999 he built a third sculpture, Omphalos, of stone and concrete, a metre and a half high. A foundation complained to the police. In August 1999 a district court ordered Omphalos removed but refused to order the removal of Nimis and Arx, and the foundation appealed to the Supreme Court and lost.

The removal of Omphalos shows how Swedish law carried on working inside the claimed country. Vilks proposed blowing it up on Nobel Day in 2001 and applied for permission. Before the decision came out, he sold it to another artist, Ernst Billgren, who asked that it not be damaged. A crane boat hired by the state enforcement office took it away on 9 December, damaging it, and Vilks was billed 92,500 kronor.

Ladonia has a queen for life, an elected president and a language of two words, "waaaaalll" and "ÿp". It takes citizenship applications online and counted 22,858 citizens in 2020, from over 50 countries, none of whom live there. The declaration brought attention, and Swedish courts and agencies decided what stayed and what went.

lanse-saint-jean.story:
L'Anse-Saint-Jean is a municipality of about 1,300 people in the Saguenay region of Quebec, Canada, founded in 1838 by lumber prospectors. From 1997 to 2000 it made itself a joke monarchy. On 21 January 1997 about 74 percent of residents voted in a referendum to create what was called the first municipal monarchy in America.

Denys Tremblay, a professor of environmental art at the Université du Québec à Chicoutimi, was crowned King Denys I at the local church on 24 June 1997, before more than 1,500 people. The parish priest crowned him, and he swore religious, civic and constitutional oaths. The arrangement was carefully fitted inside the existing law. The king was named for life but could be removed by referendum at any time, the title was not hereditary, he had no special privileges, and it cost residents nothing. The mayor acted as his representative and the council kept meeting as usual, so the town's real government did not change.

The aim was to bring in tourists and support the local economy, and in particular to fund a giant artwork in plants on Mont-Édouard, depicting Saint John the Baptist and estimated to cost about a million dollars. The monarchy also proposed a municipal currency that was really a lottery ticket organised with the Quebec naming commission, and the winner could give a place in Quebec a name of their choice.

Because the money for the artwork did not come, the project was dropped, and Tremblay abdicated on 14 January 2000 in a ceremony at the presbytery, released from his oaths by the priest with the mayor as a witness. The town remained a Quebec municipality throughout. The monarchy was legal because it left the town's real government in place.

liberstad.story:
Liberstad is a planned private city on three parcels of land totalling about 150 hectares in rural southern Norway, near the village of Bjelland and a few hours from Kristiansand. The organisers, John Holmesland and Sondre Bjellås, wanted a place in it where, in the words of the project's website, anarchism could get a physical foothold.

The idea follows the free-market writers Mises, Hayek and Rothbard. Public services such as roads and dispute settlement would be provided by private businesses and residents, with no government, minimal rules and no taxes. A company called Liberstad Drift AS was to keep the land records and act as custodian and do little else. The market would run on six rules built on the non-aggression principle, which says nobody may start force against another, and people breaking them would be shunned. Prices were not to be shown in government money, and a Liberstad currency was proposed.

They sold land from 2015, in bitcoin or Norwegian krone, at between about $9,400 for 1,000 square metres and $47,100 for 5,000 square metres. A 2017 Cointelegraph report said development would begin on 1 June if enough plots sold. The Startup Societies Foundation, a group that promotes such projects, reported that 120 people had bought land and that it would open in 2020. It said the project does not demand sovereignty of any type and described it as an experiment in how society could work. The founders say they do not need Norway's permission, though they hope for its goodwill.

A person who buys a plot still buys land in Norway, and Norwegian law and tax continue to apply. A private rule book binds only those who agree to it. Liberstad is not known to have a finished settlement or a permanent population.

llanrwst-free-borough.story:
Llanrwst is a market town of about 3,100 people on the River Conwy in north Wales, known in the past for wool, harps and clocks. In the 13th century, during the wars between Welsh and English rulers, the river was for periods the border between them. That left the town in an uncertain position, which gave rise to a local saying, "Cymru, Lloegr a Llanrwst", or "Wales, England and Llanrwst".

Its claim to separate status dates from the same period. In 1276 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the Welsh prince, declared it a free borough, a town with special privileges, placing it outside the Diocese of Llanelwy, the local church district. The town defended this privilege against the Church for decades. A list of micronations gives a second date of 1947, without further explanation, and what happened that year is not known.

Llanrwst is part of Wales and the United Kingdom, and a medieval privilege against a church district is a different thing from a claim to be a separate state.

malu-entu.story:
The Republic of Malu Entu was a state declared on Mal di Ventre, an 81-hectare island 7 km off the west coast of Sardinia in Italy. The name is a cartographers' mistake. The Sardinian "malu entu" means bad winds, and it was rendered in Italian as "mal di ventre", meaning stomach ache. The island has Roman ruins and a lighthouse and lies in a marine protected area. The British businessman John Miller had owned it since 1972.

The leader of this attempt was Salvatore "Doddore" Meloni, a former truck driver and campaigner who had earlier served nine years in prison over an alleged 1980s plot to win independence with help from Libya.

In September 2008 Meloni and his followers took over the island, as part of their effort to make Sardinia independent. He cited Kosovo, Abkhazia and South Ossetia as examples. He declared himself president, set up a residence in a blue plastic tent and declared the island tax-free, and said more than 300 people were interested in moving there. He sent drafts of the plan to the United Nations and to Italy's Prime Minister, Silvio Berlusconi.

The occupation ended in 2009. The law treated it as an ordinary land seizure. In 2012 he and five others were convicted of illegally seizing land and causing environmental damage, and he was sentenced to 20 months. He was also charged with tax evasion of 5 million euros in 2011.

He was arrested on tax charges in April 2017, began a hunger strike asking to be treated as a political prisoner, and died in hospital on 5 July 2017, aged 74, after a court in Cagliari refused to let him serve his sentence at home. The island was offered for sale in 2014. The case shows what happens when a claimant occupies land owned by someone else. The courts treated it as an illegal seizure of property, which brought a prison sentence.

maritime-republic-of-eastport.story:
The Maritime Republic of Eastport is a joke country in Eastport, a waterfront neighbourhood on a peninsula in Annapolis, Maryland, in the United States. The area was first settled in 1655, took the name Eastport in 1888 and was annexed to Annapolis in 1951. A drawbridge joins it to the rest of the city.

In January 1998 the Maryland State Highway Administration temporarily closed that bridge for repairs, which threatened local shops and restaurants with losing customers. Residents came up with the idea in a pub and declared a mock secession on 25 January 1998. By the group's own account, the aim was to find a creative way to encourage people to keep using Eastport's businesses.

The group has kept going ever since, with an annual tug of war against Annapolis, a very short run across the bridge, a yearly "Burning of the Socks" and fundraisers. Annapolis plays along with the joke, no government recognises it, and it is popular with tourists. Nobody treats it as a legal claim, and the neighbourhood's government remains the city of Annapolis.

murrawarri-republic.story:
The Murrawarri Republic is a state declared by the Murrawarri, an Aboriginal people whose traditional land crosses the border between Queensland and New South Wales in Australia. The claimed area is dry grassland, roughly triangular, about 200 km across and 250 km from north to south, reaching near Cunnamulla in the north. Most people living there now are not Indigenous.

The claim concerns sovereignty, the right of a people to govern itself. The Murrawarri argue that they never gave it up by treaty or lost it in a declared war.

They released a declaration of independence on 30 March 2013 and sent it to Queen Elizabeth II, Prime Minister Julia Gillard and the premiers of Queensland and New South Wales, giving them 21 days to respond. It asked the Crown to produce treaty documents, a deed of cession (a legal paper showing the Murrawarri gave up their sovereignty), or documents declaring war on them. Without any of these, they said, the Murrawarri had never lost the right to govern themselves.

The Crown did not reply by the deadline of 8 May 2013, and the council took that silence to confirm continued independence. Four days later it took its case to the United Nations, and it set up a Ministry of Defence. Time magazine reported that the Attorney-General's Department did not respond because it had no legal basis to do so, a view supported by the Sydney human-rights lawyer George Newhouse. A deadline set by one side has no force on the other, so the silence creates no independence in Australian law.

A Provisional Council of State of 11 members first met on 13 July 2013 at Weilmoringle, chaired by Fred Hooper. The republic's website claims 81,796 square kilometres, while a 2018 study in the Indigenous Policy Journal put the area near 22,170. It uses Australian money, and the Australian government has not acknowledged it. The same study found that the declaration has influenced similar efforts and the debate on Aboriginal sovereignty.

north-dumpling-island.story:
The Kingdom of North Dumpling is the joke name for North Dumpling Island, a two-acre island in Fishers Island Sound, in the town of Southold, New York, about a mile off the coast of Connecticut. John Winthrop bought it with neighbouring islands in 1639, and the federal government bought it in 1847 for $600 for a lighthouse, lit in 1859. The government sold the lighthouse grounds into private hands after 1959.

The inventor Dean Kamen, known for the Segway, bought it in 1986 for $2.5 million. When local officials refused his request to put up a wind turbine, he declared the island's secession from the United States. He was eventually able to build the turbine.

He calls it a kingdom and himself Lord Dumpling, with a constitution, a flag, a currency named the dumpling, an anthem that parodies "America the Beautiful" and a navy of one amphibious vehicle. Kamen says his friendship with President George H. W. Bush produced an unofficial non-aggression pact, but this is only his own claim.

The island runs on its own solar panels and a 10-kilowatt wind turbine, with a small backup engine, off the regional grid, and he changed all the lights to LEDs to cut use by 70 percent. It also has a replica of Stonehenge. The secession has no legal recognition, and the island remains in Southold, whose officials had first refused the turbine.

occupation-of-alcatraz.story:
Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay, California, best known for its federal prison, which closed on 21 March 1963. The next year the government declared it surplus property, meaning it no longer needed it. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie between the United States and the Lakota was read by them to mean that retired or abandoned federal land should go back to the Indigenous people who once held it. The island had also held Indian prisoners in the late 1800s and early 1900s, including 19 Hopi in 1895, which led one activist to say it was already Indian land in a way.

In 1963 Belva Cottier, a Rosebud Lakota social worker, read that the prison would close, and with her cousin Richard McKenzie she found a copy of the treaty. On 8 March 1964 a small group of Lakota occupied the island for four hours and proposed a cultural centre and an Indian university. A lawyer came with them to pursue a claim.

Five years later a loss brought the idea back. Plans for commercial development of the island were being discussed, and on 10 October 1969 the San Francisco Indian Center, which provided jobs, health care and legal help, burned down. Adam Fortunate Eagle planned a boat trip around the island for 9 November. Richard Oakes, an Akwesasne Mohawk, and LaNada Means, a Shoshone-Bannock student leader at Berkeley, joined with other students. Oakes and four others jumped from a yacht and swam, claiming the island by right of discovery, and the Coast Guard picked them up. That evening 14 people landed and stayed overnight. On 20 November about 100 people, 80 of them students from UCLA, began a full occupation under the name Indians of All Tribes.

They wanted the deed to the island, an Indian university, a cultural centre and a museum. They governed themselves as a community of people from many tribes, and John Trudell served as spokesman. Fresh water came by barge. Oakes left after his stepdaughter died in a fall on the island in January 1970, and as students went back to school, rival groups fought for control.

In mid-1970 it offered part of Fort Miley in San Francisco, and the occupiers refused. It cut off the electricity and removed the barge that brought fresh water, and days later a fire destroyed several buildings. President Nixon approved a removal plan, and on 10 June 1971 federal marshals, FBI agents and police removed the last 15 people. No court ever accepted the treaty claim. Oakes was shot dead in 1972.

The island did not become Indian land, and the National Park Service now runs it. The Park Service says the occupation helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes, which sought to end tribes' legal status. The case shows a government ending an occupation by controlling water and power, and the same occupation helping to change national policy.
occupation-of-alcatraz.why: The 1964 landing is given as a small group of Lakota organised by Belva Cottier and Richard McKenzie, following the full Wikipedia article, in place of five people led by Cottier.

orania.story:
Orania is a town on the Orange River in the dry Karoo region of the Northern Cape of South Africa, 871 km from Cape Town, set up for Afrikaners, the Afrikaans-speaking white South Africans. Its background is apartheid, the system of legal racial separation in South Africa, which was in its last years in 1990. Boshoff believed that black majority rule could not be stopped.

The town began as a camp for workers on irrigation canals, built by the Department of Water Affairs in 1963. Most workers left after the project, and the town fell apart in the 1980s. Mixed-race and black families squatted there. In December 1990 about 40 Afrikaner families led by Carel Boshoff bought it for around R1.5 million. Boshoff, a right-wing academic, was a son-in-law of Hendrik Verwoerd, the prime minister known as the architect of apartheid, and founded the Afrikaner Volkswag in 1984. The 64 families living there, about 500 people, were evicted by the department before the buyers moved in. The first 13 settlers arrived in April 1991, to 90 houses in poor repair. Boshoff hoped that hundreds of thousands of Afrikaners would one day live there in a state of their own, called a Volkstaat.

The legal tool is private ownership, by a company set up for the purpose. To live there, a person must apply and be accepted as an Afrikaner, speak Afrikaans, have a clean criminal record and share the group's goals. All jobs, from management to manual labour, are done by Afrikaners, on a principle of self-reliance. Founders say this rejects the old system in which white people lived off black labour. CNN and other outside observers describe the town as whites-only and as an attempt to revive apartheid, a description the community disputes. Residents say they want to preserve their culture and protect themselves from crime.

In daily life the town grows pecan nuts, has pursued energy independence through solar power and has its own sewage works. It prints money-like coupons for use in its shops, and it has tried out a cryptocurrency. It keeps the last transitional representative council in the country, a form of local government left over from the end of apartheid. In 2016 CNN reported about 1,300 residents, and a local census in December 2025 counted 2,903, with growth estimated at 10 percent a year in 2019. The council has planned for 10,000.

The relationship with the state is unusual. On 23 April 1994 the Freedom Front and the two main parties signed an accord on Afrikaner self-determination. That led to section 235 of the South African Constitution, which guarantees a right of self-determination for cultural groups, and the MK Party gave notice in March 2026 that it intends to repeal it. In 1995 President Nelson Mandela visited for tea with Verwoerd's widow and said residents were entitled to run their affairs. A minister called the ideal of an Afrikaner cultural home within the Constitution legitimate in 1998. The South African government has said it opposes a whites-only community but has generally left the town alone. After Boshoff died in 2011, his son took over the Orania Movement.

Orania remains part of South Africa. It shows how far private land purchase can go toward a separate community, including control over who lives there, and it shows that this depends on a government choosing not to force the issue against its own equality principles.

other-world-kingdom.story:
The Other World Kingdom was a commercial resort for BDSM, a form of sexual role-play based on dominance and submission, at a 16th-century château on 3 hectares in the municipality of Černá in the Czech Republic. It was founded on 1 June 1996 and opened to visitors by spring 1997 after two years of building that cost £2 million.

It presented itself as a state ruled by women under an absolute monarch, Queen Patricia I, crowned in May 1997. It claimed its own currency, passports, police, courts, flag and anthem. Its fictional law placed women above men, who were either subjects with some rights or "slaves" with none.

In fact it was a private for-profit business with no connection to any recognised state, and no country recognised it. Czech law continued to apply, so its "courts" and "police" had no public power. The property was offered for sale in 2008 for eight million euros and was still for sale in 2016. That year the queen announced a new venture and a fundraiser to buy land. As of 2020 the company still owned the building and held regular events there. The case shows the language of statehood used purely as marketing.

outer-baldonia.story:
Outer Baldonia was a joke principality on about 4 acres of Outer Bald Tusket Island, the southernmost of the Tusket Islands off the southern tip of Nova Scotia, Canada. The American businessman Russell Arundel founded it in 1949 as a private fishing retreat and took the title Prince of Princes. It had a flag, currency, passports and a joke military. Its charter, now kept at the Yarmouth County Museum, covered 69 fishermen. Anyone who caught a bluefin tuna and paid $50 became a prince.

The charter is what brought it wider attention. The Soviet publication Literaturnaya Gazeta criticised it, and Outer Baldonia declared war on the Soviet Union on 9 March 1953. Press coverage later showed the place to be a humorous half-truth.

Arundel sold the island in 1973 for one Canadian dollar to the Nova Scotia Bird Society, and it became the Earle E. Arundel Breeding Bird Sanctuary. In 2015 the Bald Islands were donated as conservation land, and in 2012 the story became a play, Whimsy State. Throughout, the land was privately owned under Canadian law, and the title ended with the sale.

parva-domus.story:
Parva Domus Magna Quies is a private social club in the upscale Punta Carretas neighbourhood of Montevideo, Uruguay, overlooking the Río de la Plata, that calls itself a republic. Its Latin name means small house, big rest. On 25 August 1878 fishermen tired of carrying their gear to the beach bought a small shack for storage and meetings and declared it a republic as a joke. It now occupies a neoclassical house built in 1919, called the presidential palace, with gardens, statues, a museum and a theatre.

It has a president elected every two years, a cabinet of ministers, a flag and an anthem, and it marches in costume on its Independence Day each August. Members take flamboyant titles. Its creed is pleasure and friendship. Members avoid talking about religion, politics and sport, and anyone who loses their temper can be put in a mock jail. Membership is all male, limited to 250 at a time, and drawn from wealthy professionals such as doctors, lawyers and politicians, and past members include the poet Juan Zorrilla de San Martín.

The joke has reached public life. Uruguay's postal service issued a stamp for its 125th anniversary in 2003. In 2007 it hosted informal talks between Argentine and Uruguayan diplomats during a dispute over a pulp mill on their shared river. It opens to the public on Uruguay's Heritage Day.

It is legally registered in Uruguay as a cultural association, and it has no official recognition as a state. It has lasted nearly 150 years as a club.

pescenica.story:
The Republic of Peščenica was a satirical country set in Peščenica, a suburb of Zagreb, the capital of Croatia. Željko Malnar, a Croatian traveller, writer and television personality, proclaimed it on 3 October 1992 and named himself president.

The republic grew out of his weekly television show Nightmare Stage, which featured colourful characters from the streets of Zagreb, and it was used to mock Croatian politics.

The show ended on 26 June 2010, which is the end date a list of micronations gives for the republic. Malnar's biography has him holding the title until his death on 9 July 2013. It is on the map as a state that existed mainly on television, and it made no legal claim a government would have to answer.

principality-of-filettino.story:
Filettino is a village of about 554 people some 70 kilometres east of Rome in Italy, which announced in 2011 it would become an independent principality. During the euro crisis that year the Italian government passed an austerity package of about 50 billion euros. To save money it required towns of fewer than 1,000 people to merge with their neighbours.

The mayor, Luca Sellari, would have lost his job under the plan, and he wanted the town to keep managing its own land, forests and water. So he led a campaign to make Filettino a self-governing principality, pointing to the many small states that existed before Italy was unified in the 19th century. The town printed a currency called the fiorito with his picture on it and sold T-shirts with a new coat of arms.

Not everyone agreed, and a local restaurant owner said residents wanted to run their own resources but not to leave Italy. How towns are organised is decided by the Italian parliament and government, and a mayor's declaration has no power over a national law. By November 2011 the merger had still not gone ahead, although the government was pressing the town to share services. What became of the principality after that is not known.

principality-of-freedonia.story:
The Principality of Freedonia was a plan to found a libertarian country, one with minimal government, based in Boston, Massachusetts, in the United States. A group of American teenagers began it in 1992 as a hypothetical project and made it a formal plan for a new country in 1997, headed by a Texas university student named John Kyle, who used the title Prince John. It minted 50-Freedonian-dollar coins of one ounce of silver and sold them on its website.

In 2001 it tried to lease land in Somaliland, a self-governing region of Somalia, and the attempt was rejected. It never gained territory beyond one leader's home. The founder said in 2004 that the project was no longer being pursued, and its website had gone by 2013. The house stayed in Massachusetts, under American law.

principality-of-marlborough.story:
The Principality of Marlborough was a short-lived state declared in 1993 near Marlborough, Queensland, Australia, about 106 kilometres north of Rockhampton. George Muirhead, a grazier, or livestock farmer, was facing the repossession of two rural properties. Repossession means a lender takes back land when a borrower does not pay. He declared the properties independent.

He named himself Duke of Marlborough and held a ceremony under four flags, which he said stood for five generations of his ancestors, those of Australia, the Aboriginal people, Scotland and the United Nations. Police evicted him and his family eleven days later, and Sydney newspapers reported in June 1993 that he and others had been jailed for contempt of court over the land. Contempt of court is the offence of disobeying a court's orders.

The declaration did not stop the repossession, and Australian police and courts enforced it within days.

principality-of-seborga.story:
Seborga is a village of 283 people (2025) in Liguria, northwest Italy, near the French border and about 35 kilometres from Monaco. It lives on olives, flowers and tourism. Italy was formed in 1861 when the House of Savoy, a royal family, united many smaller states. The claim made for Seborga is that it was left out of that process.

In 1963 Giorgio Carbone, a former flower grower who headed the local growers' cooperative, said documents in the Vatican archives showed Seborga had never belonged to the House of Savoy. So, he argued, it was wrongly included in the Kingdom of Italy. He said it had been a sovereign state since 954 and a principality of the Holy Roman Empire from 1079. Supporters add that the Congress of Vienna, the 1815 meeting that redrew Europe's borders, overlooked it. None of these claims has been proved.

Villagers elected Carbone head of state that year, and he took the title His Tremendousness, Giorgio I. He formed a cabinet, minted a currency called the luigino, and adopted a blue and white flag and the Latin motto Sub Umbra Sede, meaning sit in the shade. Sentry boxes stand on the road into the village. Supporters say Burkina Faso recognised it, which has not been confirmed. His campaign is widely viewed as a way to attract tourists. Tourism has grown, and the village centre has been restored.

He held the role until he died in 2009. Marcello Menegatto was elected in 2010 and Nina Menegatto in 2019, with a further seven-year term confirmed on 23 October 2026.

Italy continues to run the village as an ordinary comune, or municipality, in Imperia province, and no court is known to have tested the claim. The principality and the comune cover exactly the same land and exist side by side.

principality-of-wy.story:
The Principality of Wy is a family house in Mosman, a suburb of Sydney, Australia, whose owner declared it independent of the local council.

The cause was a driveway. In 1993 the Delprat family applied to build one across an unbuilt road to reach their home, which began a long dispute with Mosman Council. On 15 November 2004 the artist Paul Delprat declared that he had seceded from Mosman, though not from Australia, and named himself Prince.

The fight over the driveway carried on under ordinary planning law, and after 20 years of seeking permission he lost his court appeal in 2013. In the meantime the principality drew coverage from newspapers and broadcasters in several countries, including Sky News and The Daily Telegraph. Delprat attended the first Australian conference of micronation leaders in 2010 on Dangar Island, sponsored by Macquarie University.

It works mostly as an arts patron. It sponsors an art prize, holds exhibitions and supports emerging artists, and a character based on it appears in the Japanese comic Hetalia. It has no local, national or international recognition, and the family never got its driveway.

province-of-bumbunga.story:
The Province of Bumbunga was a four-hectare farm near Snowtown and Lochiel in South Australia that its owner declared independent so that it could stay loyal to the British Crown.

Australia's head of state is the British monarch, represented by a Governor-General. In November 1975 the Governor-General, John Kerr, dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam's government. Alec Brackstone, a British monarchist and former monkey trainer, postmaster and uranium prospector, feared that Australia was moving toward becoming a republic. To make sure part of the continent stayed loyal, on 29 March 1976 he declared the property independent and appointed himself governor-general.

To draw tourists he planted thousands of strawberry plants in the shape of Great Britain and planned weddings on soil from British counties, but Australian customs seized the imported soil and the plants later died in a drought. From 1980 he issued collectors' stamps with no postal value, mostly showing the royal family, in fifteen series of 5,000 each. They sold well to collectors. Changes to investment law in 1987 made such stamps less attractive, and he gave up the business.

In 1999 he was charged with illegally possessing firearms, and his claim to diplomatic immunity failed, though he says the charges were later dropped. Diplomatic immunity is a protection governments give to accepted foreign envoys, and Australia did not treat him as one. The claim is usually dated as ending about 2000, but Brackstone was still calling himself its governor in 2018.

rainbow-creek.story:
The Independent State of Rainbow Creek was a farm at Cowwarr, on the Thomson River in Victoria, Australia, that seceded from the state of Victoria over flooding. The name comes from a channel the river cut by itself. In the 1930s a road bridge was built too close to the flood line. In a violent flood in 1952 debris jammed against it, and the river carved a new course around it, straight through private farms. This was Rainbow Creek.

Later floods widened it, and a weir built in 1954 sent more water into it. By the late 1970s it was 8 metres deep and over 50 metres wide. The farmers were caught in the rules. They paid the council for land now under water, because their deeds did not show the creek. They paid the state water commission for using the creek's water for irrigation, and they paid a third levy to a trust meant to stop the erosion, which went on regardless. They built their own bridges, and severe floods in 1978 washed those away with crops, stock and equipment.

Thomas Barnes, a retired British and Victorian police officer who had owned the Yammacoona property below the weir since 1970, led the farmers. When they were refused compensation in 1978, Barnes and about thirty others signed a declaration of war on Victoria and served it on the state governor before television cameras in January 1979. They rejected a government offer of loans. On 23 July 1979 Barnes declared Yammacoona seceded from Victoria, named himself Governor and swore allegiance to Queen Elizabeth II, in imitation of Hutt River, a farm in Western Australia that had declared itself independent in 1970.

The state issued passports, stamps and banknotes to publicise the farmers' cause. Barnes retired to Queensland in the mid-1980s because of ill health, and the flooding dispute was never resolved. The law governing the farm did not change.

republic-of-kugelmugel.story:
The Republic of Kugelmugel is a spherical house eight metres across that its builder declared an independent country, now standing in the Prater park in Vienna, Austria. "Kugel" is German for a ball, and "Mugel" is an Austrian word for a bump or hillock. In 1971 the artist Edwin Lipburger and his son Nikolaus built it at Katzelsdorf, near Wiener Neustadt in Lower Austria, without a building permit, which started a long dispute with the authorities.

In August 1975 the township of Neudörfl offered it a home, and moving it by helicopter was discussed, but that did not happen. Lipburger then declared the sphere an independent republic, with the date given as 19 December 1976, and issued passports.

Austria's response was a specific offence. In 1979 he was sentenced to 10 weeks in prison for unlawful assumption of a public authority, the Austrian offence of acting as an official without the right to. The conviction was for acting as an official, which is a separate matter from declaring a house a country.

In 1982 the building was dismantled and moved to the Prater, where it sits behind tall barbed-wire fences. Helmut Zilk, who became mayor of Vienna in 1984, gave it what was called asylum. The city assumed the arrangement would be temporary, and the legal dispute continued, with power and water cut off. Lawsuits reached Austria's Supreme Administrative Court in 2007, and all of them failed, with no formal agreement ever reached. The city stopped trying to remove it, and it now accepts it as part of Vienna's culture, classed as a building without a permit.

The republic claims 94 square metres and has a single address, 2 Antifaschismusplatz. Lipburger died in January 2015. Leadership passed to Nikolaus Lipburger and in 2022 to Linda Treiber, as president. It reports more than 650 citizens, none living there, and since June 2024 visitors can pay for a stamped visa. The house remains in the Prater. The founder's lawsuits failed, and the city still came to accept the building.
